docs.title: wgpathd
docs.text:
wgpathd is a small ucode daemon for OpenWrt that keeps each WireGuard mesh peer on its best working path. Between two spokes it prefers a direct IPv6 path, and it falls back to a relay through the hub when the direct path does not work. It does this by rewriting one thing only: the endpoint of each mesh peer, with wg set <iface> peer <key> endpoint <addr>. The hub also runs wgpathd, in a second role: it publishes the IPv6 endpoints it sees, so that spokes know where to look for each other.

flowchart LR
    subgraph hubnode[hub]
        H[wgpathd role=hub]
    end
    A[spoke-a] -- "wg_hub (IPv4, always up)" --- hubnode
    B[spoke-b] -- "wg_hub (IPv4, always up)" --- hubnode
    A == "wg_mesh direct (IPv6)" === B
    A -. "wg_mesh relayed inside wg_hub" .-> hubnode -.-> B

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
wgpathd is for operators who already run WireGuard hub-and-spoke on OpenWrt and want site-to-site traffic to skip the hub whenever it can. It does not build your tunnels. You bring the WireGuard setup; wgpathd steers it.

Before wgpathd can do anything useful you need:

  • Two WireGuard interfaces on every node, with separate keys. wg_hub is the IPv4 tunnel from each spoke to the hub. It is always up and it carries the relay. wg_mesh is the IPv6 mesh whose peer endpoints wgpathd steers.
  • Endpoint-less mesh peers. On each spoke, every other spoke is a wg_mesh peer with no endpoint. For each, wgpathd's own configuration holds two settings, keyed by the peer's public key: its relay endpoint (where to send when relaying) and its tunnel address (the peer's address inside the tunnel, used for the health probe).
  • A hub that forwards the transit range. The hub forwards traffic between its wg_hub peers, so a spoke can reach another spoke's wg_hub address through it.
  • At least one inbound-reachable IPv6 site. A pair of spokes goes direct if at least one of them accepts inbound WireGuard over IPv6. If neither does, that pair stays on the relay.

How to prepare the WireGuard substrate walks through all of this. Whether wgpathd is the right tool for you at all, and what else to consider, is in Why wgpathd?.

docs.title: About wgpathd
docs.text: wgpathd exists to answer one question for every pair of sites, all the time: can these two talk directly, or must they go through the hub? It answers by trying, and it only ever acts by moving a WireGuard peer endpoint.

docs.title: Direct and relay
docs.text:
In a plain hub-and-spoke WireGuard setup, spoke-a reaches spoke-b through the hub. That always works, because every spoke keeps a tunnel to the hub. But it costs a detour: every byte between two sites crosses the hub, adds latency, and uses the hub's bandwidth.

When at least one of the two sites is reachable on public IPv6, the detour is unnecessary. The two spokes can hold a WireGuard session straight to each other. wgpathd calls this the direct path, and the detour the relay path. Direct is the optimization. Relay is the floor that always works.

The trick is that both paths use the same WireGuard interface and the same session. wg_mesh on spoke-a has one peer for spoke-b. What changes is only that peer's endpoint:

  • Direct: the endpoint is spoke-b's public IPv6 address, for example [2001:db8:b::20]:51820. Packets go out over the WAN.
  • Relay: the endpoint is spoke-b's address on the hub tunnel, for example 10.10.0.12:51820. That address routes into wg_hub, so the already-encrypted wg_mesh packet travels inside the hub tunnel. The hub decrypts the outer layer and forwards the inner packet to spoke-b over spoke-b's own wg_hub tunnel. The hub never sees the site traffic in clear text.
flowchart TB
    subgraph sa[spoke-a]
        am[wg_mesh peer spoke-b]
        ah[wg_hub]
    end
    subgraph hub
        hh[wg_hub, forwards 10.10.0.0/24]
    end
    subgraph sb[spoke-b]
        bm[wg_mesh listen 51820]
        bh[wg_hub]
    end
    am -- "endpoint [2001:db8:b::20]:51820<br/>over the WAN" --> bm
    am -. "endpoint 10.10.0.12:51820<br/>routed into wg_hub" .-> ah
    ah -. "outer layer" .-> hh
    hh -. "inner wg_mesh packet" .-> bh
    bh -. "arrives on port 51820" .-> bm

Since the tunnel does not change, switching paths never changes addressing, AllowedIPs or routes. The kernel keeps routing site traffic into wg_mesh; wgpathd just decides which underlay carries it.

docs.title: Data plane and control plane
docs.text:
The name hub-and-spoke can mislead. In a working wgpathd setup the data plane is spoke-to-spoke whenever direct works. Only the control plane is hub-and-spoke: the hub tells spokes where the others currently are (discovery), and it serves as the relay when direct does not work.

The two roles follow from this:

  • A spoke runs the path decision. For each mesh peer it gathers evidence, tries the direct path, proves it, and keeps checking it. See About the path state machine.
  • The hub makes no decisions. It reads its own wg_mesh peer table and publishes the IPv6 endpoints it sees over a small HTTP endpoint.

Each spoke decides only where it sends. spoke-a to spoke-b and spoke-b to spoke-a are separate decisions. For a short while one side may be direct and the other relayed. That is legal and both directions still work; there is no consensus protocol to get wrong.

docs.title: What it deliberately does not do
docs.text:
wgpathd is small because it refuses most of the job that tools like Tailscale or Netmaker take on.

  • It does not create or change interfaces. It never writes /etc/config, never touches AllowedIPs, routes, MTU or wg_hub. It checks that the interfaces it was told about exist and refuses to start otherwise. The reason is safety: the worst a wgpathd bug can do is point a mesh peer at a bad endpoint. It can never cut the hub tunnel you use to manage the router. See the trust model.
  • It does not distribute keys or peers. Which peers exist, and their keys and AllowedIPs, are static configuration you render yourself. The hub publishes only endpoints.
  • It does not do NAT traversal. There is no STUN, no hole punching, no relay protocol of its own. wgpathd assumes at least one side of a pair accepts inbound IPv6. If neither does, the pair stays on the relay, which is the correct result.
  • It does not push metrics. Per-peer state and switch counts are in the ubus call wgpathd status reply for whatever collector you already run.

docs.title: Where it sits among other tools
docs.text: Choosing between a direct and a relayed path is not a new idea. How wgpathd compares with staying on the hub, a ping-and-switch script, a routing daemon over two tunnels and full overlays such as Tailscale, and when one of those is the better choice, is in Why wgpathd?.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: wgpathd is built as a functional core with an imperative shell. One pure function makes every path decision. Everything that touches the system — ubus, commands, HTTP, sockets, routes, files, the clock — lives in a thin shell around it. This page explains that split and how one cycle runs.

docs.title: The pure core
docs.text:
The core is decide(ctl, obs, params, now) in decide.uc. For one peer, it takes:

  • ctl, the peer's control state: its RELAY/TRIALING/DIRECT state, streak counters, backoff, trial deadline, target, the endpoint wgpathd last set, and the failed trials in a row on one address and when it was given up;
  • obs, what the shell observed this cycle: the kernel's current endpoint, the underlay probe result, last cycle's tunnel probe result and the endpoint the kernel held right after its answer, the discovery candidate, the relay endpoint and the tunnel address;
  • params, the timing parameters and the mode;
  • now, the time, passed in rather than read.

It returns the next ctl and a list of effects. It does no I/O and reads no clock, so a test can replay any scenario, including the passage of minutes, instantly and exactly.

The effects form a closed vocabulary: set_endpoint, tunnel_probe, refresh_discovery, log, given_up, resumed and metric. effects.uc defines and validates it. There is no effect that could create an interface or change AllowedIPs, which is how the scope limit is enforced by structure.

docs.title: The shell
docs.text:
The shell (daemon.uc) gathers observations, calls decide for each peer, and carries out the effects. It holds no decisions of its own. All its I/O comes through a single deps object built in deps.uc, which is what lets the integration tests replace every system interface with a fake.

The I/O each part uses:

Need Mechanism Read WireGuard peer state ubus call wireguard status (from rpcd-mod-wireguard), asynchronous Set the endpoints one wg set <iface> peer <key> endpoint <addr> ... per cycle, exit code only Underlay and tunnel probes ICMP echo on raw sockets via ucode-mod-socket, on the uloop Relay and candidate route checks, mesh MTU rtnl RTM_GETROUTE and RTM_GETLINK via ucode-mod-rtnl Discovery fetch (spoke) asynchronous HTTP GET via ucode-mod-uclient Discovery server (hub) TCP listener via ucode-mod-socket on the uloop Status a wgpathd ubus object with a status method Liveness procd watchdog ping, ubus call service watchdog Configuration UCI, read at startup and on SIGHUP

The one command, wg set, runs through uloop.process with its output discarded, under a timer backstop, because a child process cannot be killed from ucode, only forgotten. A spoke therefore starts one process per cycle, however many peers it steers.

The probes are sent by the daemon itself. It keeps a raw socket per address family and device, registered on the loop, and a reply answers a probe only if it arrives on the socket the probe left by, from the address probed, with that socket's echo id, the probe's sequence number and the payload the probe carried. Each socket draws its echo id and first sequence number at random when it opens, and every probe carries 8 random bytes, read from /dev/urandom, at the start of its payload. So a late reply to an earlier probe, or a reply to someone else's ping, never counts; and a reply forged from what the underlay probes show in the clear answers nothing, because a tunnel probe travels inside the tunnel and its reply must come back out of mesh_iface. Anything else the socket receives is dropped.

Everything runs on one single-threaded uloop. Nothing blocks: the ubus read, the probes, wg set and the HTTP fetch are all callbacks.

docs.title: One spoke cycle
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    T([cycle timer fires]) --> R[recheck relay routes of peers still waiting]
    R --> V["set aside each candidate that is the router's own,<br/>the peer's relay or tunnel, or routes into a tunnel"]
    V --> G["an underlay ping to each peer in RELAY with a candidate, all at once"]
    G --> K[wireguard status]
    K --> D[decide, per peer]
    D --> S["one wg set for every peer's endpoint"]
    S --> P["tunnel pings, all at once, for the peers that asked;<br/>a wireguard status read right after answers"]
    P --> F{discovery fetch due?}
    F -- yes --> BG[start fetch in background] --> W
    F -- no --> W[ping procd watchdog]
    W --> N([arm next timer, cycle seconds later])

Some details that matter operationally:

  • A candidate is vetted once per cycle, before the probes. An address from discovery that belongs to the router, is the peer's relay or tunnel address, or routes out of mesh_iface or hub_iface is set aside for the cycle: the peer has no candidate, so it is neither probed nor trialed there. The underlay ping and decide see the same candidate. See discovery.
  • The kernel is read last, just before deciding. Every cycle re-asserts every endpoint, and a peer's direct packet may roam the kernel while the underlay pings wait. Reading wireguard status after them, rather than alongside, lets decide see such a roam before the re-assert overwrites it.
  • A tunnel probe answer belongs to the next cycle. The pings are sent right after wg set returns, and their results are stored for the next cycle's obs. If wg set fails, no probe is sent at all, since the command may have set some endpoints and not others, so a probe over the old path can never commit a trial.
  • An answer is read together with the path it came back on. The answer, like every authenticated packet, moves the kernel endpoint to where it came from, so the shell reads wireguard status right after it and stores that endpoint with the result. decide commits a trial only on an answer that came back from its target (see the state machine). Answers that arrive while such a read is in flight share the next read, which starts as soon as it returns; a read made before an answer arrived could show the endpoint from before that answer moved it, so it never serves one.
  • A cycle only waits for gathering and applying. The timer for the next cycle is armed cycle seconds after the current one finishes. With probes and wg set taking up to their timeouts, the real period is a little longer than cycle.
  • The watchdog ping is the last step. procd restarts the daemon if it has not been pinged for 30 seconds. A stuck cycle stops pinging, so a hang becomes a restart, and a restart puts every peer back on the relay.
  • An unreadable wireguard status skips deciding for that cycle. Peers keep their state and no endpoint is set. Any pending tunnel probe result is discarded, so a DIRECT peer counts a failed probe on the next cycle.

The hub's cycle is shorter: read the wireguard status of read_iface, replace the snapshot if the read worked, ping the watchdog, arm the timer. The HTTP server answers from the latest snapshot and never runs a command per request.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text:
The init script runs check.uc --config before it asks procd for an instance. The check uses the daemon's own configuration loader, so it cannot disagree with the daemon. procd respawns a daemon that exits, which is what turns a hang or a crash into a clean start on the relay; but a configuration the daemon can never load would only exit again every 5 seconds. Checking first keeps that case out of the respawn loop: the service is left without an instance and the reason is on the console and in the log.

The daemon's own startup is fail-closed:

  1. Load and validate /etc/config/wgpathd and, on a spoke, the wg_mesh peers from /etc/config/network, each matched by public key to its peer section in /etc/config/wgpathd.
  2. Check the WireGuard interface (mesh_iface or read_iface) is present in the wireguard status reply, so it exists in the kernel, not only in UCI.
  3. On a spoke, run the relay loop guard for each peer, log every unmanaged peer, and load the discovery cache.
  4. Publish the wgpathd ubus object; on the hub, also bind the discovery listener.
  5. Log started role=<role> ... and run the first cycle.

Any failure in steps 1, 2 or 4 exits with status 1 and a logged reason. procd then respawns the service after 5 seconds. These are the failures the config check cannot see, such as an interface that is not up yet, so retrying them is useful. See log messages.

docs.title: Reload
docs.text:
A restart is always safe, because every peer falls back to the relay, but it throws away evidence: a peer that was DIRECT has to earn direct again. So a configuration change is applied with SIGHUP instead. procd sends reload when the wgpathd or network configuration changes, and the init script turns it into a signal, again only after the config check passes.

On the signal the daemon loads the configuration again, with a fresh UCI cursor, and sorts the changes into two kinds:

  • Structural. role, the interfaces and the listener address and port decide what the process is: which ubus reads it makes, which socket it holds, whether it steers or publishes. Rewiring those in place would be a second startup path, so the daemon exits instead and lets procd start it afresh 5 seconds later.
  • Everything else is data the cycle reads each time: the timing parameters, the mode and the discovery URL simply take effect on the next cycle.

Peers are matched by public key, relay endpoint and tunnel address. A peer whose three values are unchanged keeps its control state, because its evidence and backoff were earned on exactly that path. A new peer, or one whose relay or tunnel changed, starts in RELAY like at startup, after the relay loop guard. A removed peer is dropped from steering and status.

If the configuration is invalid by the time the daemon reads it, the daemon logs it and keeps the configuration it has. A signal that arrives before startup completes is applied right after it.

docs.title: Module map
docs.text:
Module Role decide.uc, state.uc, effects.uc The pure core: decision, state helpers, effect vocabulary daemon.uc The shell: startup, reload, cycles, status, hub snapshot relay.uc, direct.uc The relay loop guard, shared by the daemon and the check, and the guard on direct candidates address.uc The special-purpose address ranges: where the hub may listen, and which addresses can be a direct path check.uc, status_view.uc service wgpathd check and the text of service wgpathd status firewall.uc What each role needs the firewall to accept, and whether /etc/config/firewall does, for the check rpc.uc, candidate.uc The wgpathd.config ubus object that rpcd serves (the check, the mesh peers without their keys, the parameter bounds), and unsaved values laid over the saved configuration migrate.uc The move of peer settings out of /etc/config/network, from releases up to 4 publisher.uc Hub snapshot and the HTTP request/response mapping and listener discovery.uc Spoke payload validation and the cache config.uc, params.uc Configuration loading and timing defaults wg.uc, endpoint.uc The wireguard status parser, the wg set command, the endpoint canonical form probe.uc, icmp.uc What each probe is (host, size, device), and ICMP echo on the wire deps.uc, components/ Real I/O: ubus, syslog, rtnl, uclient HTTP, command runner, ICMP prober, clock result.uc, errors.uc The ok/err result type and the error codes

Endpoints are compared as plain strings, so every endpoint that enters the core — from the kernel, discovery, the cache or the peer sections — is first put in one canonical form ([v6]:port or v4:port, lowercase and compressed, as wg prints it). Without that, the same address written two ways would look like a roam every cycle.

docs.title: How the core is tested
docs.text:
The split decides where the tests go. Every decision is in decide, so every decision is tested there, as a unit test with no I/O: build a ctl and an obs, call decide, check the next state and the effects. Time is an argument, so a test replays minutes of backoff in a few milliseconds, and the same scenario gives the same result at any starting time. The shell makes no decisions, so its integration tests only check the plumbing, with every part of deps replaced by a fake. The end-to-end suite then runs the package on real OpenWrt nodes and breaks the network under it.

Two kinds of unit test cover decide:

  • Scenarios. One test per situation wgpathd must handle, most of them the cases in When things fail: the anchor that only sees roams, the hub that lies, the path that loses one direction, and so on.
  • Invariants. Property tests feed decide long random sequences of observations and check, after every cycle, rules that must hold whatever happens. They are numbered in the test names:
Invariant I1 Every effect is in the vocabulary, with exactly one metric and at most one tunnel probe per cycle. I2 The endpoint set is the relay, a candidate seen from discovery or a roam seen in the kernel, never any other address. I3 Every cycle sets exactly one endpoint: the relay in RELAY, the target in TRIALING and DIRECT. I4 Without any sign of a direct path, every state is back in RELAY within the trial window plus m_down cycles. I5 In observe mode, only the relay is ever set and no tunnel probe is sent. I6 An answer that came back over the relay never commits a trial. I7 A trial starts only once the backoff has run out. I8 A trial commits only on an answer from its target, and DIRECT holds only on an answer. I9 Between two changes (a roam, a new candidate, the end of the pause, a committed trial), at most give_up_after trials start on the same target.

A few more properties are named by what they check rather than numbered, such as decide never changing its inputs. Each run prints the seed of its random inputs.

docs.title: About Discovery
docs.text: A spoke cannot try a direct path to a peer without knowing the peer's public IPv6 address. Roaming sites change that address. Discovery is how spokes learn it: the hub publishes the endpoints it sees, and spokes fetch them.

docs.title: Why the hub knows
docs.text:
Every spoke has the hub as a wg_mesh peer with a fixed endpoint and a persistent keepalive. The keepalive means each spoke sends the hub a packet over IPv6 at least every 25 seconds or so. WireGuard on the hub records the source address of each valid packet as that peer's endpoint. So the hub's own wg_mesh peer table always holds each spoke's current public IPv6 address and port, with no extra protocol.

The hub side of wgpathd simply reads that table once per cycle and keeps a snapshot of the peers whose endpoint is an IPv6 address that could be a direct path. It publishes the snapshot as JSON on GET /peers. It keeps no other state.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as spoke-b (roamer)
    participant H as hub
    participant A as spoke-a
    B->>H: wg_mesh keepalive over IPv6
    Note over H: kernel records spoke-b's<br/>endpoint [2001:db8:b::20]:51820
    loop every cycle
        H->>H: read wg_mesh peers,<br/>keep usable IPv6 endpoints
    end
    A->>H: GET /peers over wg_hub
    H-->>A: { spoke-b key: { direct, handshake_age } }
    Note over A: spoke-b's direct candidate is now<br/>[2001:db8:b::20]:51820
    Note over A,B: only a candidate: the probes and a trial<br/>decide whether the direct path works

The hub reads wg_mesh but serves on its wg_hub address. That split matters. wg_mesh is where the IPv6 endpoints live, so it is the only table worth reading. wg_hub is the tunnel that stays up when the mesh is broken, so serving there means discovery works exactly when it is needed.

docs.title: Soft state, never in the way
docs.text:
Discovery supplies where to probe. The probes and the trial decide whether the path works. Nothing the hub says can commit a peer to DIRECT on its own.

Because of that, discovery is allowed to be stale or missing:

  • A spoke fetches on its first cycle and then every discovery_interval (60 seconds by default). When a peer sits in RELAY with no evidence, the spoke asks for an early refresh, at most every 10 seconds. That is how a spoke picks up a peer that moved while the direct path was down.
  • The fetch runs in the background. The cycle never waits for it, so a dead hub never slows a fallback to relay.
  • A good payload replaces the known map and is saved to /var/run/wgpathd/cache.json. A failed fetch keeps the last map. On startup the spoke loads the cache, so it can probe before the first fetch succeeds.
  • The cache lives in /var/run, which is in memory. It survives a restart or an upgrade of the daemon, but not a reboot: after a reboot a spoke remembers no addresses until it reaches the hub again. It is kept out of the router's flash on purpose, to spare it a write after every fetch. The relay endpoint never comes from discovery, so an empty cache only means a spoke stays on the relay until the hub answers.

docs.title: Strict about what it accepts
docs.text:
The spoke treats the payload as untrusted input. One malformed entry rejects the whole payload, which then counts as a failed fetch. The limits are listed in the discovery HTTP API reference. Rejecting everything rather than filtering keeps a buggy or hostile hub to one effect: spokes stop learning new addresses. See the trust model for why that is the worst it can do.

A well-formed entry is a different matter when its address simply cannot be a direct path: loopback, link-local, multicast, an IPv4 address in IPv6 clothing, and the like. That is one peer's address, not a broken payload, so the spoke leaves out that entry alone and keeps the rest; the hub does not publish such an address in the first place. Unique local addresses are kept, since a private mesh over ULA is as direct as one over the internet. Then, every cycle, the spoke refuses a candidate that is right for the internet but wrong for this router: one of its own addresses, the peer's relay or tunnel address, or an address routed into wg_mesh or wg_hub, where a WireGuard endpoint would loop into a tunnel. Either way the peer just has no candidate and stays on the relay, and a probe never leaves toward such an address.

Entries for keys the spoke does not manage are ignored. The hub publishes every peer it sees, including the spoke itself; each spoke looks up only the wg_mesh public keys of its own managed peers.

docs.title: Only the roamer really needs it
docs.text: A spoke with a stable public address could, in principle, be configured statically. wgpathd does not bother. Discovery publishes every peer with a usable IPv6 endpoint, stable or not, so all spokes can share one identical wgpathd configuration. The per-peer facts that must not come from the hub, the relay address and the tunnel address, live in the static network configuration next to each peer's key.

docs.title: About the Path State Machine
docs.text: On a spoke, every managed mesh peer has its own small state machine. It has three states: RELAY, TRIALING and DIRECT. This page explains why it has those states, what moves a peer between them, and why the rules are lopsided on purpose.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> RELAY: start
    RELAY --> RELAY: re-assert relay endpoint,<br/>count evidence
    RELAY --> TRIALING: n_up cycles of evidence<br/>toward an address not given up,<br/>or a roam; backoff expired<br/>(trial_start)
    TRIALING --> TRIALING: set target, probe again
    TRIALING --> DIRECT: tunnel probe answered<br/>over the direct path<br/>(trial_ok)
    TRIALING --> RELAY: trial_window passed<br/>(trial_timeout, backoff grows,<br/>the failure counts)
    DIRECT --> DIRECT: re-assert target, probe,<br/>adopt roams
    DIRECT --> RELAY: m_down failed probes<br/>(demoted, backoff grows)
    TRIALING --> RELAY: mode set to observe<br/>(observe_mode)
    DIRECT --> RELAY: mode set to observe<br/>(observe_mode)

Every peer starts in RELAY, including after a restart. State is kept in memory only, so a restarted daemon earns direct again from scratch. That takes a few seconds and keeps the design simple. A configuration reload is gentler: it keeps the state of every peer whose settings did not change (see Architecture).

Once per cycle (every 3 seconds by default), wgpathd sets the endpoint the current state calls for: the relay endpoint in RELAY, the direct target in TRIALING and DIRECT. It does this every cycle even if nothing changed. wg set ... endpoint does not rekey or interrupt the session, so re-asserting is harmless.

docs.title: Evidence first, then proof
docs.text:
A direct path needs two different kinds of support before wgpathd commits to it.

Evidence is cheap and gathered every cycle. There are two kinds:

  • Underlay echo. wgpathd pings the peer's public IPv6 address (the candidate learned from discovery) outside the tunnel. A reply means the peer's host is reachable on IPv6. Only a peer in RELAY is pinged: that is the only state in which the echo decides anything.
  • Authenticated roam. WireGuard moves a peer's endpoint to the source address of the last valid packet from that peer. If the kernel shows an endpoint that is neither what wgpathd set nor the relay, the peer has just reached us directly, and it did so with a packet that passed its static key. Nobody can fake that without the key.

A peer needs n_up consecutive cycles of evidence (5 by default, about 15 seconds) before a trial may start. A roam is the exception: one is enough, for reasons explained below.

Evidence is not proof. A host can answer ICMP while its firewall drops UDP to the WireGuard port. So the next step is a trial: wgpathd sets the endpoint to the direct target and immediately sends a ping to the peer's tunnel address, through wg_mesh. Only an answer to that ping, coming back over the direct path, commits the peer to DIRECT. It proves the whole path works, in both directions, for real WireGuard traffic.

Why a round trip, and not "wait for a new handshake"? Because changing an endpoint does not start a handshake. The session keys stay the same, and the kernel only rekeys every two minutes or after sends go unanswered. A trial that waited for a handshake would fail on good paths and bad paths alike. So wgpathd never uses handshake age to decide anything; it is shown in the hub's discovery data for diagnosis only.

In DIRECT, the same tunnel ping runs every cycle. It is the health check, and it also keeps the session and any stateful firewall on the path warm.

The tunnel ping is as large as wg_mesh allows: the whole packet fills the interface's MTU, and it is never fragmented on the way out. A direct path that carries small packets but loses large ones, such as a link with a smaller MTU that drops them instead of reporting it, would pass a small ping while real traffic stalls. With a full-size ping such a path fails its trial or its health check, and the peer stays on, or returns to, the relay. The ping is also bound to wg_mesh, so whatever the routes say, it can only leave through the tunnel.

docs.title: Relay traffic and the proof
docs.text:
WireGuard roams on every authenticated packet, and that includes packets that come through the relay. Suppose spoke-b trials while spoke-a is still in RELAY and its site is sending traffic. wgpathd on spoke-b sets the direct endpoint, and a moment later a packet from spoke-a arrives through the hub and moves spoke-b's endpoint straight back to the relay. The trial ping then leaves through the relay, spoke-a answers it through the relay, and the answer says nothing about the direct path. Counting it would commit DIRECT on a path that may be dead, and on a dead path the daemon would then re-assert the dead endpoint every cycle and never back off.

So a trial's answer only counts if it came back from the trial's target. The answer is itself an authenticated packet: it moves the kernel endpoint to wherever it came from. wgpathd reads the endpoint right after the answer arrives. If that is not the target, the relay included, the trial carries on, setting the target and probing again each cycle, and times out with a backoff if no answer comes back from the target before the deadline. Requiring the target and not merely some direct address matters because the trial is about to commit to it: an answer from elsewhere proves a path, not the one DIRECT would then assert. If the peer moves to a new direct address in the middle of a trial, the trial therefore times out, and the next one, after the backoff, can start on the new address.

DIRECT does not apply this rule: any answer keeps the peer DIRECT, whichever path the read shows. While the other side is still in RELAY and sending, as it is during a trial of its own, in observe mode or in backoff, its relayed packets move our endpoint back onto the relay within a millisecond of nearly every direct answer, and more so the slower the relay is than the direct path. Measured in the lab with steady traffic from a side held in RELAY, applying the rule in DIRECT demoted a healthy direct path again and again, whatever the relay delay, and with 20 ms of added relay delay the two sides mostly never converged. The price of the looser rule: a path that dies while DIRECT, with the other side sending through the relay, can keep answering over the relay and stay DIRECT. Traffic still flows, since every relayed packet moves the endpoint back onto the relay, but the state is wrong; relayed_answers in the status keeps growing while that lasts. A roam to another direct address is followed in the next cycle.

The endpoint is read right after the answer, not at the start of the next cycle, on purpose. A peer in RELAY re-asserts its relay endpoint every cycle. If it has traffic to send, its next packet comes through the relay and moves our endpoint back there, well before our next cycle begins. A check made then would reject every answer while the other side is in RELAY, even on a healthy path, and two sides whose backoffs run out at different times could each wait for the other forever.

A trial is still at the mercy of timing under heavy traffic from the other side: if a relayed packet lands between wg set and the ping, the ping itself goes through the relay. The trial then simply tries again on its next cycle.

docs.title: What a trial costs
docs.text:
A trial is not free. A WireGuard peer has one endpoint, so while a trial runs, all traffic to that peer takes the candidate path. On a good path the probe answers on the next cycle and nothing is lost. On a bad one, that peer's traffic is lost until the trial window ends, up to trial_window (8 seconds by default), and then it returns to the relay.

There is no cheaper test. WireGuard ignores unauthenticated packets, so nothing outside the tunnel can prove a path works, and one peer cannot use two endpoints at once.

The cost repeats when the evidence is misleading: a peer that answers ICMPv6 echo while a firewall blocks UDP to its WireGuard port, or an address that is stale or wrong but still answers ping. The echo keeps producing evidence, so each backoff expiry would start another trial and lose another window: with the backoff at its cap of 15 minutes, about 1% of that peer's traffic, for as long as the address stays. Giving up an address bounds that. A failed trial keeps the peer on its target until the first cycle at or after trial_window: 9 seconds with the defaults. The worst cases, with the defaults, over a day:

Case What it costs A fixed address that answers ping but never carries WireGuard give_up_after trials within the first few minutes, then one each time give_up_pause runs out: 6 trials, 54 seconds, in the first day (0.06%). Without giving up it was about 99 trials, 15 minutes (1%). A hub that publishes another bad address on every fetch Every address is new, so none is given up, and the backoff alone bounds it: one trial per backoff, backoff_max once it has grown, about 1% as before. A hub can already hold its spokes on the relay by publishing nothing, so a lying hub gains nothing new. A good address after a long outage that let ping through but not WireGuard The address was given up during the outage. Once the path is back, the peer stays on the relay until its pause runs out, at most give_up_pause (6 hours), unless the other side's packets arrive directly first, the hub publishes another address, or the daemon restarts. The cost is time on the relay; no traffic is lost.

An outage that stops ping as well costs nothing of the kind: without evidence no trial runs and nothing is counted, so the first trial after the path is back commits.

docs.title: Giving up an address
docs.text:
After give_up_after trials in a row on the same address time out (3 by default), wgpathd gives that address up. It logs direct address given up, and the peer's status shows it under given_up. From then on:

  • The underlay echo alone starts no trial toward that address. The peer stays on the relay.
  • A trial starts again, backoff permitting, only when something changes. wgpathd logs direct address trials resumed with the reason:
    • roam: the peer's own packets arrive directly, an authenticated roam. As always, the trial starts at once and takes the roam's source as its target.
    • new_candidate: discovery offers another address for the peer, and it answers the echo. A different port makes a different address.
    • pause_over: give_up_pause (6 hours by default) has passed since the address was given up. The echo may start one more trial toward it.
  • If the trial toward the same address fails again, after the pause or after a roam from that address, the address is given up again at once, without give_up_after more failures, and the pause starts over.

Only a trial that times out counts, against its target: the endpoint with its port. A timeout on another target starts the count again at one: wgpathd keeps a count for one address per peer at a time, so once another address has been tried, the one given up before gets give_up_after trials again. A trial that commits clears the count.

A demotion from DIRECT is not counted. A path that passed its trial carried the peer's packets both ways, so the address is right; what failed is the path, for a while, and a failing path is what the backoff is for. Even a path that passes every trial and dies right after costs no more than before: m_down failed probes per backoff, the backoff growing to its cap. Counting those demotions would give a correct address up and keep the peer on the relay for the whole pause.

The underlay probe keeps running while an address is given up. It is one small ping per cycle, it shows in the status whether the address still answers, and the evidence it keeps counting lets the trial after the pause start at once.

Giving up applies whether discovery is fresh or not. Candidates never expire, and the cache keeps them through a hub outage on purpose: a remembered address that is still right lets two spokes find each other while the hub is down. Giving up bounds what a remembered address that has gone wrong can cost.

Observe mode never trials, so it never counts a failure. A peer whose address is given up is not ready, since steer mode would not trial it. The count and the give-up are kept in memory with the rest of the peer's state: a reload keeps them for every peer whose settings did not change, and a restart of the daemon forgets them, which is the way to retry at once.

Two spokes can give each other's address up, as when a firewall filters the path in both directions. When one of them retries at the end of its pause and the path works again, its trial's packets reach the other directly, a roam, so the other trials at once and both return to DIRECT together.

docs.title: Why the anchor needs roams
docs.text:
Picture the common case. spoke-a is the anchor: it accepts inbound IPv6. spoke-b is a roamer behind a stateful firewall that drops unsolicited traffic.

  • spoke-b pings spoke-a's public address. spoke-a answers. spoke-b has evidence, trials, and goes DIRECT.
  • spoke-a pings spoke-b's public address. spoke-b's firewall drops it. spoke-a never gets echo evidence.

If echo were the only evidence, spoke-a would stay on the relay forever. It does not, because spoke-b's trial and health pings arrive at spoke-a directly. Each one roams spoke-a's kernel endpoint to spoke-b's direct address. spoke-a reads that roam as evidence and trials toward the roamed address at once, without waiting for n_up cycles, and goes DIRECT too.

One roam is enough because it is authenticated proof that spoke-b is sending to spoke-a directly right now, and because waiting would defeat spoke-b. Until spoke-a trials, it re-asserts the relay every cycle, and its site's traffic then reaches spoke-b through the relay and pulls spoke-b's endpoint back onto it. Under steady traffic, spoke-b's pings reach spoke-a directly only now and then. A streak of n_up roams could take far longer than spoke-b's trial window. The trial still has to pass, and the backoff still applies.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as spoke-a (anchor)
    participant B as spoke-b (roamer)
    A-xB: underlay ping (dropped by spoke-b's firewall)
    B->>A: underlay ping to spoke-a's public address
    A-->>B: echo reply
    Note over B: n_up cycles of echo evidence,<br/>then a trial toward spoke-a
    B->>A: tunnel ping over the direct path
    Note over A: kernel roams spoke-b's endpoint<br/>to its direct address
    A-->>B: reply, sent to the roamed address
    Note over A: roam seen: a trial toward<br/>the roamed address
    Note over B: DIRECT (trial_ok)
    A->>B: tunnel ping over the direct path
    B-->>A: reply
    Note over A: DIRECT (trial_ok)

This is also why wgpathd reads roams before it re-asserts. A daemon that blindly overwrote the endpoint every cycle would fight WireGuard's per-packet roaming instead of learning from it.

In DIRECT, a roam to a new direct address is adopted as the new target, logged as a roam event. This is how a spoke follows a peer that changes address while direct is healthy, with no dip to the relay. A roam to the relay address is not adopted: it only means the other side is relaying for now. If the probe's answer came back through the relay as well, it counts as a failed probe (see Relay traffic and the proof).

docs.title: Fast down, slow up
docs.text:
The rules are asymmetric on purpose.

  • Falling back is fast. In DIRECT, m_down failed tunnel probes in a row (2 by default) demote the peer to RELAY. Each probe's answer is read on the next cycle, and on a dead path every cycle also waits for its probes to time out, so with the defaults a dead path is left in roughly 8 to 15 seconds. A probe that did not complete in time counts as failed, and so does one answered through the relay. The relay is the safe place to be when in doubt.
  • Coming back is slow. A return to direct needs n_up cycles of evidence (or a roam from a peer that is already trialing or DIRECT) and a successful trial, and the backoff must have expired. The echo alone starts no trial toward an address that has been given up.

The backoff is what stops a flapping path from bouncing. Each failed trial and each demotion bumps it: the first time to backoff_min (30 seconds), then doubling each time up to backoff_max (15 minutes). It resets only after DIRECT has held for backoff_reset (10 minutes). A path that works for a minute and then breaks walks its backoff up to the cap and ends up parked on the relay, which is the outcome you want from a bad path. Evidence keeps counting during the backoff, so a peer that is ready trials as soon as the backoff ends.

A quiet link is never demoted for being quiet. DIRECT is judged only by the tunnel probe, which wgpathd sends itself, never by traffic or handshake age.

docs.title: Corner cases
docs.text:
A few rules settle what the diagram leaves open:

  • The first cycle judges no roam. wgpathd has set nothing yet, so whatever endpoint the kernel holds is not a roam. The first cycle sets the relay.
  • The deadline comes first. An answer that arrives in the cycle at or after trial_window is a timeout, not a commit.
  • A demotion beats a roam. If a DIRECT peer reaches m_down failed probes in the same cycle a roam shows up, it is demoted; the roam can start a trial once the backoff allows.
  • Every transition starts the streaks over. Evidence counts only in RELAY, and a new trial needs a fresh n_up streak, which may build up while the backoff runs.

docs.title: Observe and steer
docs.text:
A spoke runs in one of two modes.

In steer mode the state machine runs as described.

In observe mode a peer never leaves RELAY and no tunnel probes are sent. Evidence is still gathered and counted, and the status reports ready: true, and the log ready, steer would trial, when a peer has enough evidence that steer mode would start a trial. This lets you watch what wgpathd would do on a live network before you let it move traffic. Observe is the default, and any unknown mode value is treated as observe.

Observe mode is not hands-off. A managed peer is still set to its relay endpoint every cycle. The whole point of observe is that every managed peer sits on the known-good floor while you watch. Switching a DIRECT peer back to observe demotes it to RELAY, without a backoff, with the reason observe_mode.

docs.title: When things fail
docs.text:
The rules above were worked out against the ways a mesh breaks. What a spoke does in each, with the default parameters:

What fails What wgpathd does The hub's discovery server stops, the hub is otherwise up Spokes keep the addresses they last fetched. DIRECT peers stay DIRECT, and the relay still works. The whole hub goes down Direct sessions are peer to peer and keep working. A peer that changes address is still followed through its authenticated roam. Pairs that were on the relay lose connectivity until the hub is back. wg_hub goes down, the direct path is healthy Direct paths are unaffected; spokes run on their cached addresses. The hub publishes a wrong address The trial gets no answer, the peer returns to the relay with a backoff, and the address is given up after give_up_after failures. See the trust model. The hub sends a malformed peer list The whole payload is rejected and the last good addresses are kept. See discovery. Only one side of a pair accepts inbound IPv6 Both sides go DIRECT: one on its echo, the other on the roams it sees. See why the anchor needs roams. Neither side accepts inbound IPv6 Neither has evidence, so both stay on the relay for good. That is the correct result, not a fault. The direct path works in one direction only The trial's round trip fails, so the peer never commits, and the address is given up. The direct path drops large packets only The full-size tunnel probe fails, so the peer stays on, or returns to, the relay. The direct path flaps Each demotion grows the backoff, and the peer ends up parked on the relay. The other side sends through the relay during a trial Its packets can pull the probe onto the relay; only an answer that came back from the target commits. See relay traffic and the proof. A spoke boots with the hub down and no cache Every peer is set to its relay endpoint, which comes from local configuration and never from the hub. The daemon crashes procd starts it again, and every peer starts in RELAY. The daemon hangs It stops pinging the procd watchdog, procd restarts it after 30 seconds, and every peer starts in RELAY. See architecture.

The decision core's tests are named after these cases, and the end-to-end suite reproduces most of them on real OpenWrt nodes. See how the core is tested.

docs.title: Trust Model
docs.text: wgpathd runs on routers that you manage over the same tunnels it steers. A bug or a hostile party must never be able to lock you out, read your traffic, or redirect it. This page explains how the design keeps those promises, and what it assumes.

docs.title: The hub is not trusted with anything that matters
docs.text:
The hub is usually a rented VPS, the most exposed machine in the setup. wgpathd is built so that a compromised hub can deny service, and nothing more.

  • It cannot read site traffic. On wg_mesh the hub's AllowedIPs for each spoke cover only that spoke's tunnel address, never its site networks. When the hub relays, it forwards wg_mesh packets that are still encrypted end to end between the two spokes.
  • It cannot redirect traffic. The hub publishes only candidate endpoints. A spoke uses a candidate only after its own tunnel probe gets an answer from the peer, and that answer has to come through a WireGuard session keyed with the peer's static key. An endpoint that leads anywhere else fails the trial, and the peer returns to the relay with a growing backoff.
  • It cannot move the floor. The relay endpoint of each peer comes from the spoke's own configuration (the relay of its peer section), never from discovery. A spoke with no discovery at all, even at a cold boot with the hub down, can always set every peer to relay.
  • It cannot confuse the parser. A discovery payload that breaks any limit is rejected as a whole. See discovery.
  • It cannot aim the probes inside the router or the tunnels. A published address that is loopback, link-local, multicast or otherwise no place for a direct path is ignored, and so is one that belongs to the spoke itself, is the peer's relay or tunnel address, or routes into wg_mesh or wg_hub.

What a hostile hub can do is stop relaying, stop publishing, or publish wrong addresses. Direct paths that already work keep working without it. Pairs that need the relay lose connectivity until the hub is back, which is true of any hub-and-spoke network.

docs.title: Endpoints only
docs.text:
wgpathd's one mutating action is wg set <mesh_iface> peer <key> endpoint <addr>. The core that makes decisions can only produce a fixed set of effects: set an endpoint, send a tunnel probe, ask for a discovery refresh, log, and report a metric. No effect exists for creating interfaces, changing AllowedIPs, touching routes, or writing configuration. So the scope limit holds by construction, not by care. See architecture.

The practical meaning: the worst a wgpathd bug can do is point a mesh peer at a wrong endpoint. That peer degrades to the relay, or at worst stops working over wg_mesh. The wg_hub tunnel, which you use to reach the router, is never touched.

docs.title: Why it never creates interfaces or distributes identities
docs.text:
Tools in this space often manage the whole overlay: they generate keys, hand out peers and addresses, and create interfaces. wgpathd deliberately does none of that.

  • Creating or rewriting interfaces would mean writing /etc/config/network. A bug there could take down wg_hub, the tunnel you need to fix the bug. The daemon never writes it. The one program of the package that does is the migration from releases up to 4, which, after an upgrade, deletes the two options those releases kept on peer sections, wgpathd_relay and wgpathd_tunnel, and nothing else.
  • Distributing peers or keys through the hub would make the hub a source of identity. Then a compromised hub could add a peer or widen AllowedIPs, and read traffic. Keeping keys and AllowedIPs in static configuration, rendered by you, keeps the hub out of that path entirely.

So wgpathd is a tenant, not a landlord. You own the substrate. wgpathd checks at startup that the interfaces it was told about exist and refuses to run if they do not; service wgpathd check runs the same checks on demand. Each mesh peer it would steer must have valid settings in wgpathd's own configuration, found by the peer's public key; a peer that does not is left alone and reported as unmanaged.

The same line runs through the LuCI pages. /etc/config/network holds the private key of every WireGuard interface on the router, so the luci-app-wgpathd ACL grants no access to it at all: a peer's settings live in /etc/config/wgpathd, and the pages name the peers through a read-only rpcd method that returns each peer's section name, public key and description, and nothing else. See Files and dependencies.

docs.title: Relay loop guard
docs.text: A relay endpoint must route into wg_hub. If it routed into wg_mesh instead, relayed packets would loop into the tunnel they are supposed to carry. At startup, and again each cycle for peers still waiting, wgpathd looks up the route to each peer's relay address. A peer whose relay route leaves via mesh_iface is left unmanaged, with the reason relay routes into <mesh_iface>, and is guarded again on every reload.

docs.title: Authenticated roams
docs.text: Roams count as evidence because they are authenticated. The kernel only moves a peer's endpoint after a packet from that address decrypted correctly with the peer's key. An attacker who can spoof source addresses cannot cause a roam without the key.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
The package never touches the firewall: it ships no rules, and nothing in it writes /etc/config/firewall or loads rules. What wgpathd needs to be accepted, you add as ordinary traffic rules in your own zones, where your zone policy and your other rules still apply to them (How to open the firewall for wgpathd). service wgpathd check only reads the firewall configuration, to say which of them it finds.

Earlier releases shipped their own accepts instead, ahead of every zone rule, so that the probes and the relay worked as soon as the package was installed. A security review found what that costs: rules the operator never wrote, on every WireGuard interface of the router, and an unlimited ICMPv6 accept from the internet that a flood could use to keep the daemon busy. OpenWrt's own packages do not ship accept rules either.

What the rules expose, per role:

  • A spoke answers ICMP echo requests from the zone of wg_mesh, and takes UDP to its wg_mesh listen port from the zone of wg_hub. With both interfaces in a zone of their own, only the hub and the other spokes can send either, since only a key holder can get a packet out of a WireGuard interface. The listen port was already open to the whole internet for WireGuard itself, which answers nothing without a valid handshake.
  • A spoke also answers ICMPv6 echo requests from the internet, through OpenWrt's default Allow-ICMPv6-Input, rate-limited: the same answers any OpenWrt router with that rule gives.
  • The hub takes TCP on serve_port from the zone of the interface that holds serve_addr. The peer list it serves holds the spokes' public endpoints, which the members of the mesh already see; see below for why the zone matters.

Put the WireGuard interfaces in a zone that holds nothing else, and these rules open nothing to a LAN or to the internet.

docs.title: Why wgpathd runs as root
docs.text:
Like most OpenWrt services, wgpathd runs as root rather than as a jailed, unprivileged user. It has to hold the network-admin capability to run wg set, and that capability alone already lets a process rewrite routes, firewall rules and interfaces, so a jail would protect little that matters. What limits the damage instead is the narrow input surface: a spoke rejects any discovery payload that is not fully valid, and the hub's discovery server answers one fixed request with data that is already public to the mesh.

Where that server can be reached is partly up to you. wgpathd binds it to the one address in serve_addr and refuses a wildcard, a host name or a multicast address there, so it never listens on every interface at once. It does not make sure that the address belongs to a WireGuard interface: the configuration says which address, not which interface, and service wgpathd check only warns when no WireGuard interface in /etc/config/network has it. The firewall decides the rest: the rule the check asks for accepts the port from the zone of the hub tunnel only, but a zone that accepts all input, such as LAN by default, reaches the server as well, since the router takes a packet for any of its addresses on any interface.

docs.title: About Versioned Documentation
docs.text: The documentation describes a package that people install and then keep running for months. A router on last year's release should be able to read the docs of last year's release, and a reader who just arrived should land on the newest. This page explains how the publishing setup serves both, and why it is stricter than it first looks. The machinery itself is described in Documentation publishing.

docs.title: One version per minor, and only one maintained
docs.text:
The site has a folder per minor release, /0.1/, /0.2/, and /latest/ for the newest. Patch releases do not get their own folder; they overwrite their minor. A patch release changes behaviour in small ways at most, and a reader choosing between 0.2.0, 0.2.1 and 0.2.2 in a version selector gains nothing but a longer list. The title of each version still shows the exact release it was built from.

wgpathd is a small project, and it maintains exactly one version: the newest. That shapes the docs too. Old versions stay online, because someone is running them, but they are frozen at their last publish. Only the newest version's docs get fixes. Backporting doc fixes to every old minor would be a promise the project cannot keep, and a half-kept promise is worse than a clear rule: a reader of /0.1/ knows it is a record of 0.1, not a living page.

The other half of the rule is that the docs of unreleased work are never published. main often describes behaviour no release has yet. Publishing it, even under a dev label, would put the most visible, most search-indexed pages ahead of the code people can actually install. So main and pull requests only build the site, strictly, to catch broken links early; they never publish it. The docs go online with the release they describe.

docs.title: Why the docs branches exist
docs.text:
A release tag is immutable, and so are the docs inside it. But the docs of a release will have mistakes: a typo, a wrong default, a missing step. Waiting for the next release to fix them leaves readers with the error for weeks, and cutting a release just for a doc fix spends a version number on something that is not a change to the package.

A docs/X.Y branch is the way out. It starts at the release tag, vX.Y.0, and carries doc fixes on top of it. Pushing it republishes /X.Y/. The branch is not a release branch and never becomes one: it exists only to let the published docs of a released version get better without a new release.

docs.title: Why the branch must stay docs-only
docs.text:
The danger of a branch that sits next to a release is that it slowly becomes one. A small code fix gets cherry-picked "just this once", the docs describe it, and now the published docs of 0.2 describe code that is not in any 0.2 package. Anyone reading them and running the real 0.2 sees something else. Worse, the branch now holds a version of the code that no tag names, and nobody can say which fixes it has.

The guard makes that impossible rather than discouraged. Before a docs branch publishes, it compares the branch with its release tag and refuses if anything outside the docs changed. The code in a docs branch is therefore always exactly the code of a release, and the only way to ship a code fix is a release, with a tag, a version number and a changelog entry. The refusal message says as much: "code fixes need a release".

The guard also insists that the newest release tag of the minor is an ancestor of the branch. After a patch release, the branch has to move onto the new tag before it can publish again. Otherwise a docs fix pushed to an old branch would overwrite the patch release's docs with the docs of the previous patch, silently undoing whatever the patch changed.

Tags are not guarded. A tag is the release; its docs are by definition the docs of that release.

docs.title: Why fixes go to main first, and why never rebase
docs.text:
A doc fix that only lands on the docs branch is lost at the next minor, which is cut from main. Landing it on main first and cherry-picking it onto the docs branch keeps main the one place every fix lives, and makes the docs branch a strict subset: its release, plus a few commits that are already on main.

Merging or rebasing main into the docs branch looks like a shortcut, but it brings along everything else on main, including the docs of unreleased features. The guard catches the code that comes with them, but not the docs, which it allows by design. Cherry-picking is deliberate: each commit that reaches a published version was chosen for it.

Merging a patch release's tag into the docs branch is a different thing. The tag is a release, so everything it brings has shipped. That is why moving the branch to a patch tag is a fast-forward or a merge, while main never goes in.

When the next minor ships, its branch takes over and the old one is frozen. Nothing stops a push to the old branch, but the one-maintained-version rule means there is no reason to.

docs.title: Why latest only moves forward
docs.text:
latest is what most readers see. It must always be the newest release, whatever order publishes happen in. Publishes do happen out of order: a fix to an older version, or a manual republish of one, can run after the newer minor has shipped. If every publish took latest, republishing 0.1 would silently point the whole site back at an old release.

So a publish takes latest only if its version is the newest one on gh-pages. The comparison is by version, not by text, because 0.10 is newer than 0.9 and a text sort says otherwise. Publishes also run one at a time, since two mike deploys racing on the same branch could each overwrite the other's work.

docs.title: Pinned links and latest links
docs.text:
A link to the docs is either about the project now or about a particular release. The README and a forum answer are about now: they should follow the project, so they link to /latest/. A changelog entry, a release note, or a URL inside the package is about one release, and has to keep pointing at the docs of that release after newer ones come out.

The package matters most. A router running 0.1 that shows a help URL should lead to the 0.1 docs, where the options and messages match what is installed, not to the newest docs, which may describe options it does not have. Pinning the shipped links to the package's minor gives every installed version a link to its own docs.

Pinned links rot silently: bump the version and forget one link, and the next release ships pointing at the previous minor. A check in make lint catches that. The changelog gets the same check per section, and [Unreleased] allows no pinned link at all, because the version it will be released as is not known yet.

Links between pages of the docs are always relative. A relative link resolves inside whatever version the reader is in, so each published version is self-contained without any rewriting.

docs.title: The redirect for old links
docs.text: A link without a version, /<site>/how-to/..., is an easy one to write by hand, and any link from before the site was versioned looks like that. Nothing lives at those paths any more. Rather than breaking every such link, the site's 404 page moves a missing unversioned path under /latest/, keeping its query and anchor. A path that is already inside a version folder is left as a real "not found": redirecting it could loop, and a page that does not exist in 0.1 should not quietly become a page of another version.

docs.title: Why mkdocs.yml stays free of mike
docs.text: The versioned settings live in their own file, mkdocs.mike.yml, which inherits mkdocs.yml. With the mike plugin and version provider in the main config, a plain mkdocs serve would show a version selector with nothing behind it, and every writer's preview would depend on mike. Keeping them apart means writing and previewing the docs needs nothing but MkDocs Material, and the versioned build is exercised on its own in CI and by make -C docs build-mike.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
latest is a copy. mike can make an alias a symlink, a redirect page, or a copy. GitHub Pages cannot be relied on to serve symlinks, and redirect pages would make every /latest/ URL a hop through a stub. A copy gives real pages at stable URLs. The price is that every page of the newest version exists twice; the canonical URL of each page points to its /latest/ copy, so search engines can treat the two as one. Identical files are stored once in git, so the copy costs little on gh-pages.

The 404 redirect assumes a project site. It treats the first path segment as the site, which matches https://<user>.github.io/<site>/. On a custom domain or a user site, where the docs live at the root, the redirect would need changing.

CI and local builds use different installs. Local builds run the pinned mkdocs-material image, plus mike in a derived image. The publish job installs the same pinned mkdocs-material and mike with pip on the runner, which spares CI building the image, but their own dependencies are not pinned. A dependency release can therefore make CI's build differ from a local one. Both builds are strict, so the likely failure is a loud one, not a quiet difference in the published site.

The freeze is a rule, not a lock. Nothing technical stops a push to an old docs branch; the guard only keeps it docs-only. The project relies on the one-maintained-version rule for the rest.

docs.title: Why wgpathd?
docs.text: If your sites already talk through a WireGuard hub, wgpathd lets pairs of sites talk directly whenever they can, and fall back to the hub whenever they cannot, without changing the tunnels you already run. This page is about when that is worth having, and when another tool is the better choice.

docs.title: What going direct buys
docs.text:
In plain hub-and-spoke, every byte between two sites crosses the hub. Taking the hub out of that path gives three things, in order of how much you can count on them:

  • Sites keep talking when the hub is down. A direct session is peer to peer. Once two sites are direct, a hub outage, reboot or upgrade does not touch the traffic between them. This is the benefit that does not depend on anyone's ISP.
  • The hub carries less. Site-to-site traffic stops using the hub's bandwidth and CPU. On a small VPS with a traffic allowance, every pair that goes direct is traffic the hub no longer pays for.
  • Latency, sometimes. Direct is shorter only when the ISPs route it that way. On one real pair of sites the direct path measured about 13 ms against 25 ms through the hub; after one site's ISP renumbered it, the same pair measured about 23 ms against 24 ms. Treat lower latency as a bonus, not the reason.

docs.title: Staying on the hub
docs.text: The simplest setup, and the right one if the hub is close, reliable and not short of bandwidth. wgpathd keeps it as its floor: every peer can always go back to the hub, using a relay endpoint from local configuration that nothing on the network can change.

docs.title: A script that pings and runs wg set
docs.text:
This is the usual answer on OpenWrt. A ping-and-switch script works on a good day. What it tends to miss is what makes the switch safe:

  • A reply is not proof of the path. A ping through the tunnel can be answered over the hub, because the other side's traffic through the hub pulls the endpoint back there, so the reply proves the peer is alive, not that the direct path works. wgpathd commits only when the answer comes back over the direct path itself, with a full-size packet. See evidence first, then proof.
  • Addresses move. Home ISPs renumber IPv6 prefixes. A script with the other site's address written into it breaks quietly when that happens. wgpathd learns current addresses from the hub, see discovery.
  • Paths flap, and some addresses never work. Without hysteresis a marginal path switches back and forth; without a limit a stale address is retried forever. wgpathd drops fast, recovers slowly, and gives up on an address that keeps failing.

docs.title: A routing daemon over two tunnels
docs.text:
The classic routing answer: give each pair of sites a direct tunnel as well as the path through the hub, and let Babel or BIRD pick by metric. It is robust and well understood, and if you already run a routing daemon between your sites, adding a direct tunnel there may be all you need.

It costs more moving parts: an extra interface and extra addresses for every pair of sites, a routing daemon on every node, and route changes on every switch. And it still does not know where the other site is. The direct tunnel's endpoint is static configuration, so when an ISP renumbers a site's IPv6 prefix, that tunnel dies until someone edits it.

wgpathd works the other way round. There is one tunnel per pair and routes never change; only the endpoint moves, and the hub publishes where each site currently is.

docs.title: A full overlay: Tailscale, Netmaker, Nebula, ZeroTier
docs.text:
These do far more than wgpathd: NAT traversal for pairs where neither side is reachable, key distribution, access control, many nodes joining and leaving. If you need any of that, use one of them.

The price is their own control plane, either a hosted service or a server you run (Headscale for Tailscale, the Netmaker server), and their own daemon, which is heavy on a router with little flash. They also replace your WireGuard configuration rather than steer it.

wgpathd is a deliberately small, self-hosted slice of the same pattern:

  • It steers the kernel WireGuard you already run. There is no second overlay, no userspace WireGuard and no daemon from another ecosystem, just one ucode process.
  • It needs no outside control plane. The coordinator is the hub reading its own WireGuard peer table and serving it over a tunnel you already trust. There are no accounts and no cloud service.
  • It stays small enough to read. A daemon whose only action is wg set ... endpoint can be read in an afternoon, and it is tested end to end.

docs.title: What keeps it small
docs.text:
wgpathd makes one assumption: a pair of sites goes direct only when at least one side, the anchor, accepts inbound WireGuard over IPv6. The heavy machinery of the full overlays (STUN, hole punching, relay protocols) exists for pairs where neither side is reachable. With an anchor, the question shrinks to whether a round trip crosses the direct path. Many home connections that sit behind IPv4 carrier-grade NAT have public IPv6, so the assumption holds more often than it used to.

The other limit is scope. wgpathd changes endpoints and nothing else, so the worst a bug can do is send a peer to a bad address; it can never cut the hub tunnel you use to manage the router. See the trust model.

docs.title: When to choose something else
docs.text:
• Neither site of a pair accepts inbound IPv6. wgpathd keeps that pair on the hub, which is correct but gains nothing. A full overlay with NAT traversal can do better.
  • Many sites, or sites that come and go. wgpathd expects peers, keys and AllowedIPs to be configuration you render yourself. An overlay that distributes them fits better.
  • You already run a routing daemon between sites. Add a direct tunnel there instead of a second mechanism.
  • The hub is close, reliable and has bandwidth to spare, and you do not mind losing site-to-site traffic when it is down. Staying on the hub is simpler.

For a handful of OpenWrt sites, a WireGuard hub you already run, and at least one site on public IPv6, wgpathd is the lighter choice.

docs.title: How to Apply Configuration Changes
docs.text: wgpathd picks up changes to /etc/config/wgpathd, its peer sections included, and to the WireGuard peers in /etc/config/network on a reload, without losing the state of the peers you did not touch.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • wgpathd is configured and running: How to configure the hub or How to configure a spoke.

docs.title: 1. Make the change
docs.text:
Edit the file, or use uci. For example, to switch a spoke to steer mode:

uci set wgpathd.main.mode='steer'
uci commit wgpathd

If you changed WireGuard peers in /etc/config/network, also apply them to the interface with service network reload.

docs.title: 2. Check it
docs.text:
service wgpathd check

Fix every FAIL line. A reload refuses a configuration that fails, and the daemon keeps running with the old one.

docs.title: 3. Reload
docs.text:
service wgpathd reload

If you apply changes with LuCI's Save & Apply, or with reload_config, this happens by itself.

docs.title: 4. Confirm
docs.text:
logread -e wgpathd | tail -n 5
  • configuration reloaded peers_kept=2 added=1 removed=0: the change is live. Kept peers carry on as they were; added and changed peers start in RELAY. The peer <section> (<key prefix>): added, changed or removed lines just before it name them.
  • reload: exiting for procd to start afresh changed=mesh_iface, then stopped, and about 5 seconds later started role=spoke ...: the change needed a new process. Every peer starts again in RELAY.
  • invalid configuration, keeping the running one: the check failed. Go back to step 2.

Which changes apply live and which need a new process is listed in Service commands.

docs.title: When to restart instead
docs.text:
Run service wgpathd restart when you want the daemon to start from scratch, with every peer back on the relay, earning direct again.

An upgrade restarts a running daemon by itself, and a reload re-checks peers rejected with relay routes into wg_mesh, so neither needs a manual restart.

docs.title: To turn the service off or on
docs.text:
uci set wgpathd.main.enabled='0'
uci commit wgpathd
service wgpathd reload

The reload stops the daemon, and it will not start at boot while enabled is 0. Set it back to 1 and reload to start it again. Each peer keeps the endpoint it had when the daemon stopped.

docs.title: How to Check Mesh Paths in LuCI
docs.text:
This guide shows how to see, in the LuCI web interface, which path each mesh peer uses and why. It needs the luci-app-wgpathd package, which make package builds next to wgpathd as bin/luci-app-wgpathd-0.1.0-r8.apk. Copy it to the router and install it as in Installing wgpathd:

apk add --allow-untrusted /tmp/luci-app-wgpathd-0.1.0-r8.apk

Then log in to LuCI again, so it shows the new menu entries.

docs.title: Open the page
docs.text:
Go to Status → Mesh paths. The page refreshes by itself; there is no need to reload it.

If it says The wgpathd service is not running, enable and check the service under Network → Mesh paths (How to configure mesh paths in LuCI), or follow The service is not running.

docs.title: Read the path of each peer
docs.text:
The Peers table has one row per steered peer:

Label Path drawn Meaning Direct this router ─ peer, solid Traffic goes straight to the peer's public IPv6 address. Via hub this router ┄ hub ┄ peer, dashed Traffic is relayed through the hub. Testing direct this router ··· peer, dotted wgpathd is trying the direct path; it goes back to the hub if the test gets no answer.

Endpoint is the address WireGuard sends to now, For how long the peer has been in this state, and Switches how many times it changed state since the service started.

Peers that wgpathd does not steer are greyed out, with the reason next to them. A peer is missing from peers says how to fix each reason.

docs.title: Find out why a peer uses the hub
docs.text:
Click Show details on the peer's row. For a peer via the hub you see:

  • the direct address it tried last, and the one the hub publishes now;
  • if this router does not try the published address, why not: it is one of this router's own addresses, the peer's relay endpoint or tunnel address, or it is routed into wg_mesh or wg_hub. See Discovery HTTP API;
  • why it uses the hub, for example that a number of checks in a row got no answer over the direct path;
  • when it tries the direct path next. After each failed try it waits longer, up to the backoff_max of Timing parameters.

After several failed tests in a row on the same address, 3 by default, the row gets a Direct given up label. The details then say after how many failed tests, and when wgpathd tries the address again: once its pause of 6 hours by default is over, or as soon as the hub publishes another address or the peer reaches this router directly. The direct address is given up explains why, and how to retry at once.

For a peer testing the direct path, the details say when the test ends.

Recent changes lists the last 20 changes of all peers, newest first. The list is kept in memory since the service started; the system log has every change.

docs.title: Notice observe mode and a stale peer list
docs.text:
• In observe mode a note at the top says so. Every peer stays on the hub; a Would test direct label marks the peers steer mode would try, and a Direct given up label the peers whose address an earlier run in steer mode gave up, which steer mode would not try yet. See Moving a Spoke from Observe to Steer.
  • If the spoke cannot fetch the peer list from the hub, a warning says how old the last good list is. The Service table shows the list's address and age.

docs.title: Glance at it from the Overview
docs.text: Status → Overview has a short Mesh paths section with the path and state of each steered peer, what happens next, such as when a given-up direct address is tried again, and a Details link to the full page. It is hidden while the service is not running, on a hub, and when no peer is steered.

docs.title: On the hub
docs.text: On the hub the page lists the Published peers: the direct address the hub publishes for each spoke, and how long ago the hub last heard from it. A spoke not heard from for more than 3 minutes is greyed out.

docs.title: How to Configure the Hub
docs.text: On the hub, wgpathd reads the wg_mesh peer table and publishes the spokes' IPv6 endpoints on its wg_hub address. It steers nothing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• wgpathd is installed: How to install wgpathd.
  • The hub has wg_mesh and wg_hub as in How to prepare the WireGuard substrate, and spokes are handshaking on wg_mesh.
  • The hub's firewall accepts the spokes' peer list requests: How to open the firewall for wgpathd.

docs.title: 1. Write the configuration
docs.text:
Replace the contents of /etc/config/wgpathd with:

config wgpathd 'main'
    option enabled    '1'
    option role       'hub'
    option read_iface 'wg_mesh'
    option serve_addr '10.10.0.1'
    option serve_port '7780'
  • read_iface is the interface whose peer endpoints are published: the mesh, where the spokes' IPv6 endpoints appear.
  • serve_addr is the hub's own address on wg_hub. Spokes reach it through the tunnel that stays up when the mesh is down.
  • serve_port is the TCP port of the list, the one the hub's firewall rule accepts from the zone of wg_hub.

Every option is described in UCI configuration.

docs.title: 2. Check the configuration
docs.text:
service wgpathd check

ok    config: hub, reads wg_mesh, serves 10.10.0.1:7780
ok    wg_mesh: up, 2 peers
ok    firewall: TCP port 7780 (peer list) from wg_hub (zone vpn): accepted

Fix every FAIL line before you go on. A warn firewall: line means the spokes cannot fetch the list yet; it comes with the rule to add. Each line is explained in Service commands.

docs.title: 3. Start the service
docs.text:
service wgpathd start
service wgpathd status

running
role: hub
published peers:
  SpokeAme  [2001:db8:a::1]:51820   handshake 12s ago
  SpokeBme  [2001:db8:b::20]:51820  handshake 7s ago

The log has a started role=hub line. If the first line is not running, or wgpathd: cannot read status follows it, look at logread -e wgpathd | tail -n 5 and find the code in Log messages. A common one is startup failed: PUBLISHER_LISTEN_FAILED (...: bind(): Address not available): serve_addr is not an address of this host, or wg_hub is not up.

docs.title: 4. Check what is published
docs.text:
Each spoke should be listed under published peers with a direct IPv6 endpoint. From a spoke, fetch the same data over wg_hub:

uclient-fetch -qO- http://10.10.0.1:7780/peers

A spoke missing from the list has no IPv6 endpoint in the hub's wg_mesh table. Check that spoke's wg_mesh peer for the hub has an IPv6 endpoint and persistent_keepalive.

docs.title: How to Configure Mesh Paths in LuCI
docs.text: This guide sets up wgpathd from the LuCI web interface instead of /etc/config/wgpathd: the role, the peers a spoke steers and, if you need them, the timing parameters. The page checks the settings before it applies them.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• wgpathd and luci-app-wgpathd are installed: How to install wgpathd and How to check mesh paths in LuCI.
  • The WireGuard interfaces and their peers are set up, as in How to prepare the WireGuard substrate. The page chooses among them; it does not create them.
  • The firewall accepts what wgpathd needs, as in How to open the firewall for wgpathd. The check below says what is missing.

docs.title: 1. Open the page
docs.text:
Go to Network → Mesh paths. The page works whether or not the service runs; a note at the top says when it does not.
