If a note says This router has no WireGuard interface yet, set up the interfaces first.

docs.title: 2. Choose the role on the General tab
docs.text:
Tick Enable, then choose the Role. The tab shows only the fields of that role.

On a spoke:

  • Mode: start with Observe, which watches the paths but never switches them. Switch to Steer once Status → Mesh paths shows what wgpathd would do.
  • Mesh interface: the interface whose peers wgpathd steers, for example wg_mesh.
  • Hub interface: the interface to the hub, for example wg_hub.
  • Peer list URL: the hub's address on the hub interface, its port and /peers, for example http://10.10.0.1:7780/peers.

On the hub:

  • Mesh interface: the interface whose peers the hub publishes.
  • Publish on and Port: the hub's address on the spokes' tunnel, and a port, so that only the spokes reach the list.

docs.title: 3. Give each peer a relay endpoint and a tunnel address
docs.text:
On a spoke, open the Peers tab. It lists every peer of the mesh interface, by its section name and description in the network configuration.

For each peer to steer, fill in:

  • Relay endpoint: the peer's address on the hub tunnel and its mesh listen port, for example 10.10.0.12:51820.
  • Tunnel address: the peer's address inside the mesh, which must be in its allowed IPs, for example 10.20.0.12.

Steered says what saving the row would do. It shows Yes once both fields hold values wgpathd takes. Otherwise it shows No and, under it, why: a field is empty, a value is not valid, such as a relay endpoint with port 0, or the last check failed the peer. To stop steering a peer, clear both fields.

A peer with a fixed endpoint in its WireGuard settings (endpoint_host) and no settings here, such as the hub, shows Fixed endpoint instead of the fields, and No, it keeps its fixed endpoint under Steered. Leave the hub so. Another spoke may have a fixed endpoint too, as when a roaming site keeps the stable address of an anchor site: click Steer this peer to show its fields and fill them in. Steered then says Yes, in place of its fixed endpoint: wgpathd sets the peer's endpoint from then on. A peer with a fixed endpoint and settings shows its fields from the start. Clearing both stops steering it; the peer gets its fixed endpoint back when its interface next comes up.

docs.title: 4. Change timing only if you need to
docs.text: The Timing tab has one field per parameter, with its default shown in the empty field. Leave a field empty to keep the default. A value outside the parameter's bounds is marked at once. How to tune timing parameters says when to change them.

docs.title: 5. Check, then save and apply
docs.text:
Click Check configuration. The Configuration check list says, line by line, what wgpathd makes of the values in the form, saved or not:

Label Meaning OK As it should be. Warn Works, but worth a look, such as a relay route that could not be looked up yet. Skip Left alone on purpose, such as a peer without settings. Fail wgpathd would refuse the configuration, or leave the peer unsteered.

Each Fail marks its field in red, and the page opens the tab that holds the first one. A peer's Fail also shows under Steered, until you change the field it is about or check again. Fix the fields and check again.

The last lines are about the firewall: whether it accepts the tunnel probe and relayed packets on a spoke, and the peer list requests on the hub. A Warn there shows the rule to add under it, as commands to run on the router and as the section of /etc/config/firewall; add it under Network → Firewall → Traffic Rules, as in How to open the firewall for wgpathd. These warnings never stop Save & Apply.

Then click Save & Apply. It runs the same check first. If a line fails, it saves and applies nothing and says so above the list. Otherwise LuCI applies the change, and the running service reloads it. Look at Status → Mesh paths to see the peers.

docs.title: Let another LuCI login use the page
docs.text:
The page needs the luci-app-wgpathd ACL, which grants /etc/config/wgpathd and the wgpathd ubus objects but nothing of /etc/config/network (Files and dependencies). For a login other than root, add the ACL to its section in /etc/config/rpcd, with rpcd's unauthenticated group and luci-base, which every LuCI login needs:

config login
    option username 'meshadmin'
    option password '$p$meshadmin'
    list read 'unauthenticated'
    list read 'luci-base'
    list read 'luci-app-wgpathd'
    list write 'luci-base'
    list write 'luci-app-wgpathd'

$p$meshadmin takes the password of the system user meshadmin. Then run service rpcd reload.

docs.title: How to Configure a Spoke
docs.text: On a spoke, wgpathd steers the endpoint of each wg_mesh peer you give a relay endpoint and a tunnel address. This guide starts it in observe mode, where every managed peer is held on its relay endpoint while wgpathd reports what it would do. Turning on steering is a separate step. To do it in the LuCI web interface instead, see How to configure mesh paths in LuCI.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• wgpathd is installed: How to install wgpathd.
  • The spoke's wg_mesh and wg_hub are set up as in How to prepare the WireGuard substrate.
  • Every spoke's firewall answers the others' tunnel probes and accepts relayed packets: How to open the firewall for wgpathd.
  • The hub is configured: How to configure the hub.

docs.title: 1. Write the configuration
docs.text:
Replace the contents of /etc/config/wgpathd with:

config wgpathd 'main'
    option enabled    '1'
    option role       'spoke'
    option mesh_iface 'wg_mesh'
    option hub_iface  'wg_hub'
    option discovery  'http://10.10.0.1:7780/peers'
    option mode       'observe'

config peer
    option public_key 'SpokeBmeshPublicKeyExample00000000000000000='
    option relay      '10.10.0.12:51820'
    option tunnel     '10.20.0.12'

discovery is the hub's serve_addr and serve_port with the path /peers.

Add one peer section for each other spoke:

  • public_key is that spoke's key, as in its wg_mesh peer section in /etc/config/network. Print it with uci get network.spoke_b.public_key.
  • relay is that spoke's transit address plus its wg_mesh listen port.
  • tunnel is its tunnel address, which must be in its allowed_ips.

Give the hub peer no peer section: wgpathd leaves it alone, at the fixed endpoint of its endpoint_host. Another spoke's peer may have an endpoint_host too, a roamer's peer for an anchor for instance: its peer section makes wgpathd steer it all the same, in place of that fixed endpoint.

Every option is described in UCI configuration, and the peer section in Peer sections.

docs.title: 2. Check the configuration
docs.text:
service wgpathd check

ok    config: spoke, mode observe, 1 steered peer, 1 not steered
ok    wg_mesh: up, 2 peers
ok    wg_hub: up, 1 peer
ok    peer spoke_b: relay 10.10.0.12:51820 via wg_hub, probes 10.20.0.12
skip  peer hub: not steered (fixed endpoint)
ok    firewall: ICMP echo-request (tunnel probe) from wg_mesh (zone vpn): accepted
ok    firewall: UDP port 51820 (relayed WireGuard) from wg_hub (zone vpn): accepted
ok    firewall: ICMPv6 echo-request (underlay probe) from zone wan: accepted

There should be one ok peer line per other spoke, with its relay via wg_hub. The hub peer is always skip, with its fixed endpoint and no peer section. The firewall: lines say whether this spoke's firewall accepts what the other spokes send it; a warning comes with the rule to add (How to open the firewall for wgpathd). Fix every FAIL and warn line before you go on; Service commands explains each one, and Managed and unmanaged peers the peer reasons.

docs.title: 3. Start the service and check the relay path
docs.text:
service wgpathd start
service wgpathd status

Within a few seconds every managed peer is on its relay endpoint:

running
role: spoke (mode observe)
discovery: fresh (last success 2s ago)
peers:
  spoke_b  SpokeBme  RELAY  10.10.0.12:51820  no change yet  0 switches
unmanaged:
  hub  HubMeshP  fixed endpoint

Each peer should be in RELAY with its relay as the endpoint, and discovery should be fresh. The log has a matching started role=spoke mode=observe managed=1 unmanaged=1 line. If the first line is not running, look at logread -e wgpathd | tail -n 5 and find the code in Log messages.

Then prove the relay carries traffic, using the other spoke's tunnel address:

ping -c3 10.20.0.12

If this fails, the relay floor does not work yet, and there is no point in turning on steering. Check that the hub forwards the transit range, and that service wgpathd check on the other spoke shows its firewall accepting relayed packets and the tunnel probe.

docs.title: 4. Watch for readiness
docs.text:
Leave the spoke in observe mode for a while and watch ready and up_streak for each peer in ubus call wgpathd status. ready: true means the peer has enough direct evidence that steer mode would start a trial.

A peer that never becomes ready has no direct evidence. For an anchor, that is normal until the other side steers: its evidence is the other side's direct traffic. For a roamer, check that discovery.fresh is true and that the peer's IPv6 address answers ping -6.

When the relay works and peers become ready, continue with How to move a spoke from observe to steer.

docs.title: How to Move a Spoke from Observe to Steer
docs.text: In steer mode, wgpathd moves a peer to its direct path once it has evidence and the path passes a trial. This guide switches a spoke over and checks the result.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The spoke runs in observe mode and the relay path works: How to configure a spoke.
  • You have a way into the spoke that does not depend on wg_mesh, such as wg_hub or the LAN. wgpathd never touches wg_hub.

docs.title: 1. Switch the mode
docs.text:
uci set wgpathd.main.mode='steer'
uci commit wgpathd
service wgpathd reload

The reload keeps each peer's evidence. A peer that is already ready starts a trial on the next cycle; the others need about n_up cycles of evidence first (15 seconds with the defaults).

If you have one anchor and one or more roamers, switch the roamers first. An anchor gets its evidence from the roamers' direct traffic, so it has nothing to act on until a roamer steers.

docs.title: 2. Watch the transitions
docs.text:
logread -f -e wgpathd

A peer going direct logs:

peer spoke_b (SpokeBme): transition RELAY -> TRIALING reason=trial_start endpoint=[2001:db8:b::20]:51820
peer spoke_b (SpokeBme): transition TRIALING -> DIRECT reason=trial_ok endpoint=[2001:db8:b::20]:51820

reason=trial_timeout instead of trial_ok means the tunnel probe got no answer over the direct path within trial_window. The peer is back on the relay and backs off for 30 seconds, doubling on each further failure.

docs.title: 3. Check the status
docs.text:
service wgpathd status

A direct peer shows DIRECT, with the peer's IPv6 endpoint and (trial_ok) as the reason of its last change:

  spoke_b  SpokeBme  DIRECT  [2001:db8:b::20]:51820  12s ago (trial_ok)  2 switches

Confirm on the wire with wg show wg_mesh endpoints.

Once both spokes of a pair steer, both should settle in DIRECT. For a short time one side may be DIRECT while the other is still RELAY; both directions keep working.

docs.title: 4. Go back to observe
docs.text:
To stop steering, set the mode back and reload:

uci set wgpathd.main.mode='observe'
uci commit wgpathd
service wgpathd reload

Every managed peer returns to its relay endpoint on the next cycle, logged as transition DIRECT -> RELAY reason=observe_mode.

For what to do when a peer does not go direct, or keeps falling back, see How to inspect status and troubleshoot.

docs.title: How to Install wgpathd
docs.text: wgpathd is one architecture-independent .apk package for OpenWrt 25.12 and later. Install the same package on the hub and on every spoke; the role is chosen in configuration afterwards.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The WireGuard substrate is in place: How to prepare the WireGuard substrate.
  • The firewall accepts what wgpathd needs: How to open the firewall for wgpathd. The package adds no firewall rules.
  • The router can reach its package feeds, so apk can pull in the dependencies.
  • A checkout of the wgpathd repository and Docker on your workstation, to build the package.

docs.title: 1. Build the package
docs.text:
In the repository:

make package

This builds bin/wgpathd-0.1.0-r8.apk in the OpenWrt SDK, inside Docker. See How to build the package for other versions and checks.

docs.title: 2. Copy it to the router
docs.text:
scp bin/wgpathd-0.1.0-r8.apk root@192.0.2.1:/tmp/

If the router has no SFTP server, add -O to use the legacy SCP protocol.

docs.title: 3. Install it
docs.text:
On the router:

apk update
apk add --allow-untrusted /tmp/wgpathd-0.1.0-r8.apk

--allow-untrusted is needed because a locally built package is not signed with a key the router trusts. The dependencies come from the regular feeds; the full list is in Files and dependencies.

docs.title: 4. Check the result
docs.text:
The package ships its configuration with enabled '0', so nothing runs until you configure a role:

service wgpathd status

active with no instances
disabled (option enabled in /etc/config/wgpathd)

Installing reloads rpcd, which then serves the configuration check over ubus, daemon or not:

ubus call wgpathd.config check

Until you configure a role, the answer has "ok": false and a finding config: option role must be 'spoke' or 'hub' (is unset). See ubus config check.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• On the hub: How to configure the hub.
  • On each spoke: How to configure a spoke.

docs.title: To upgrade
docs.text:
From release 5 or earlier: add the firewall rules first

Releases up to 5 loaded wgpathd's firewall accepts themselves; this one does not, and the upgrade removes them from the running firewall. On every node, add the rules of How to open the firewall for wgpathd before you upgrade it. Otherwise a zone that rejects input rejects wgpathd's probes, relayed packets and peer list from the moment the upgrade finishes.

Build and copy the new package, then run apk add --allow-untrusted on it as above. Your /etc/config/wgpathd is kept, and a running daemon is restarted on the new code. Every peer starts again in RELAY and earns direct within a few cycles. After an upgrade from release 5 or earlier, run service wgpathd check and make sure no firewall: line is a warning.

Releases up to 4 kept each peer's relay endpoint and tunnel address in /etc/config/network. An upgrade from one of them moves those settings into /etc/config/wgpathd before the daemon restarts; How to upgrade from a release that kept peer settings in the network configuration shows how to check that it did.

docs.title: How to Open the Firewall for wgpathd
docs.text:
The wgpathd package ships no firewall rules. This guide adds the few that wgpathd needs, as ordinary traffic rules in /etc/config/firewall, and confirms them with service wgpathd check. Do it on every node, before you turn wgpathd on.

Upgrading from release 5 or earlier

Releases up to 5 loaded these accepts themselves, from a firewall include that the upgrade removes. Add the rules below before you upgrade such a node. Otherwise, once the upgrade reloads the firewall, a zone that rejects input rejects wgpathd's probes, relayed packets and peer list, and every peer falls back to the relay, or loses the relay too.

The examples follow How to prepare the WireGuard substrate: wg_mesh and wg_hub are both in a zone called vpn, wg_mesh listens on UDP 51820, and the hub publishes its peer list on 10.10.0.1:7780. Use your own zone names and ports.

docs.title: What each role needs
docs.text:
Role Traffic Arrives on Rule Spoke ICMP echo requests: the other spokes' tunnel probes The zone of mesh_iface Allow-wgpathd-tunnel-probe Spoke UDP to the wg_mesh listen port: relayed WireGuard packets The zone of hub_iface Allow-wgpathd-relay Spoke ICMPv6 echo requests: the other spokes' underlay probes The wan zone OpenWrt's own Allow-ICMPv6-Input, which a default configuration has: keep it Hub TCP to serve_port: the spokes' peer list requests The zone of the interface that holds serve_addr Allow-wgpathd-discovery

A zone whose input policy is already ACCEPT needs no rule. Why each one is needed, and what the check can confirm, is in Firewall rules.

WireGuard itself needs its listen ports open from WAN; How to prepare the WireGuard substrate does that, and it is not repeated here.

docs.title: 1. Find the zones of the interfaces
docs.text:
uci show firewall | grep -e '\.name=' -e '\.network=' -e '\.device='

firewall.@zone[0].name='lan'
firewall.@zone[0].network='lan'
firewall.@zone[1].name='wan'
firewall.@zone[1].network='wan' 'wan6'
firewall.@zone[2].name='vpn'
firewall.@zone[2].network='wg_hub' 'wg_mesh'

A zone may name devices instead, as in firewall.@zone[2].device='wg_hub' 'wg_mesh': a WireGuard interface's device has the interface's name, so that zone holds both interfaces too. In LuCI the same is under Network → Firewall, in the Zones list. If an interface is in no zone, add it to one first, under Network → Firewall → Zones, Edit, Covered networks, or with uci add_list firewall.@zone[2].network='wg_mesh'.

docs.title: 2. Add the rules of a spoke
docs.text:
LuCIuci/etc/config/firewall

Go to Network → Firewall → Traffic Rules and click Add for each rule:

Field Tunnel probe Relayed packets Name Allow-wgpathd-tunnel-probe Allow-wgpathd-relay Protocol ICMP UDP Source zone the zone of wg_mesh the zone of wg_hub Destination zone Device (input) Device (input) Destination port — 51820 Action accept accept Advanced Settings → Restrict to address family IPv4 only — Advanced Settings → Match ICMP type echo-request —

Click Save, then Save & Apply.

uci add firewall rule
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].name='Allow-wgpathd-tunnel-probe'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].src='vpn'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].proto='icmp'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].icmp_type='echo-request'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].family='ipv4'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].target='ACCEPT'

uci add firewall rule
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].name='Allow-wgpathd-relay'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].src='vpn'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].proto='udp'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].dest_port='51820'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].target='ACCEPT'

uci commit firewall
service firewall reload

config rule
    option name 'Allow-wgpathd-tunnel-probe'
    option src 'vpn'
    option proto 'icmp'
    option icmp_type 'echo-request'
    option family 'ipv4'
    option target 'ACCEPT'

config rule
    option name 'Allow-wgpathd-relay'
    option src 'vpn'
    option proto 'udp'
    option dest_port '51820'
    option target 'ACCEPT'

Then run service firewall reload.

  • The tunnel probe goes to the spoke's own address on wg_mesh. If that address is IPv6, choose IPv6 only (family 'ipv6') instead; if the interface has addresses of both families, leave the family out.
  • The relay rule's port is the listen_port of this spoke's own wg_mesh, the port the other spokes put in its relay endpoint.
  • If wg_mesh and wg_hub are in different zones, give each rule the zone of its own interface.

A new rule goes to the end of the list. If a rule above it rejects the same traffic, move the new one above that rule: in LuCI, drag it; the check says when this is the case.

docs.title: 3. Keep OpenWrt's ICMPv6 rule on a spoke
docs.text:
Other spokes find out whether a spoke's public IPv6 address answers by pinging it, from the internet. OpenWrt's default configuration accepts that ICMPv6 echo request on wan with its rule Allow-ICMPv6-Input, rate-limited to 1000 packets a second, so wgpathd needs no rule of its own for it.

Check that the rule is still there: Allow-ICMPv6-Input in the Traffic Rules list, with Enable ticked and echo-request among its ICMP types. If you removed or narrowed it, restore it. The check in step 5 confirms it too.

docs.title: 4. Add the rule of the hub
docs.text:
LuCIuci/etc/config/firewall

Go to Network → Firewall → Traffic Rules and click Add:

Field Value Name Allow-wgpathd-discovery Protocol TCP Source zone the zone of wg_hub, the interface that holds serve_addr Destination zone Device (input) Destination port 7780, your serve_port Action accept

Click Save, then Save & Apply.

uci add firewall rule
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].name='Allow-wgpathd-discovery'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].src='vpn'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].proto='tcp'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].dest_port='7780'
uci set firewall.@rule[-1].target='ACCEPT'
uci commit firewall
service firewall reload

config rule
    option name 'Allow-wgpathd-discovery'
    option src 'vpn'
    option proto 'tcp'
    option dest_port '7780'
    option target 'ACCEPT'

Then run service firewall reload.

Accept the port from the hub tunnel's zone only. From any other zone, the peer list would be open to whatever that zone reaches.

docs.title: 5. Confirm with the check
docs.text:
Once wgpathd has a role, service wgpathd check looks for each of these rules. On a spoke:

service wgpathd check

ok    config: spoke, mode observe, 1 steered peer, 1 not steered
ok    wg_mesh: up, 2 peers
ok    wg_hub: up, 1 peer
ok    peer spoke_b: relay 10.10.0.12:51820 via wg_hub, probes 10.20.0.12
skip  peer hub: not steered (fixed endpoint)
ok    firewall: ICMP echo-request (tunnel probe) from wg_mesh (zone vpn): accepted
ok    firewall: UDP port 51820 (relayed WireGuard) from wg_hub (zone vpn): accepted
ok    firewall: ICMPv6 echo-request (underlay probe) from zone wan: accepted

On the hub, the last line is ok firewall: TCP port 7780 (peer list) from wg_hub (zone vpn): accepted.

A rule that is missing gives a warn line instead, followed by the rule to add, both as uci commands and as the section of /etc/config/firewall:

warn  firewall: UDP port 51820 (relayed WireGuard) from wg_hub (zone vpn): no rule accepts it
      add it with:
        uci add firewall rule
        uci set firewall.@rule[-1].name='Allow-wgpathd-relay'
        ...

The Check configuration button of Network → Mesh paths in LuCI shows the same lines, with the rule under each warning.

could not confirm means the check cannot tell, for example because a rule has conditions it does not follow, or the firewall has custom nftables rules. The traffic may well be accepted: look at the rule or the custom rules it names, or add the rule it suggests to be sure. The firewall findings are never FAIL, so they do not stop the service or LuCI's Save & Apply. Every message is listed in Service commands.

docs.title: How to Prepare the WireGuard Substrate
docs.text:
This guide sets up the WireGuard interfaces that wgpathd steers. wgpathd never creates or edits them; it checks they exist and refuses to start otherwise. Do this once per node, before you install wgpathd.

The examples use one hub and two spokes. spoke-a accepts inbound IPv6 (the anchor); spoke-b does not (a roamer). Replace every key and address with your own.

hub spoke-a spoke-b Public address 203.0.113.10, 2001:db8:ff::1 2001:db8:a::1 changes wg_hub address (transit) 10.10.0.1/24 10.10.0.11/32 10.10.0.12/32 wg_mesh address (tunnel) 10.20.0.1/32 10.20.0.11/32 10.20.0.12/32 Site network — 10.11.0.0/16 10.12.0.0/16

If you already run hub-and-spoke on one interface, that interface can be your wg_hub. Keep its name; wgpathd only needs to be told which it is.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Generate two keypairs per node, one for wg_hub and one for wg_mesh. Do not reuse a key across interfaces.
  • Give the mesh interface a fixed listen port on every node, 51820 in the examples: the other spokes' relay endpoints name it, and the firewall accepts relayed packets on it. The examples call the interfaces wg_hub and wg_mesh, but any names work: you tell wgpathd which is which.
  • Keep the wg_mesh MTU at least 60 bytes below the wg_hub MTU, so a relayed packet fits inside the hub tunnel. The examples use 1360 inside the default 1420.

docs.title: 1. Configure the hub
docs.text:
Add both interfaces to /etc/config/network on the hub.

config interface 'wg_hub'
    option proto 'wireguard'
    option private_key '<hub wg_hub private key>'
    option listen_port '51830'
    list addresses '10.10.0.1/24'

config wireguard_wg_hub 'spoke_a_transit'
    option public_key 'SpokeAhubPublicKeyExample000000000000000000='
    list allowed_ips '10.10.0.11/32'

config wireguard_wg_hub 'spoke_b_transit'
    option public_key 'SpokeBhubPublicKeyExample000000000000000000='
    list allowed_ips '10.10.0.12/32'

config interface 'wg_mesh'
    option proto 'wireguard'
    option private_key '<hub wg_mesh private key>'
    option listen_port '51820'
    option mtu '1360'
    list addresses '10.20.0.1/32'

config wireguard_wg_mesh 'spoke_a'
    option public_key 'SpokeAmeshPublicKeyExample00000000000000000='
    list allowed_ips '10.20.0.11/32'
    option route_allowed_ips '1'

config wireguard_wg_mesh 'spoke_b'
    option public_key 'SpokeBmeshPublicKeyExample00000000000000000='
    list allowed_ips '10.20.0.12/32'
    option route_allowed_ips '1'

Section names must be unique in the whole file, even across section types: UCI refuses a wireguard_wg_mesh 'spoke_a' next to a wireguard_wg_hub 'spoke_a'. The examples add _transit to the wg_hub peers.

On wg_mesh, give each spoke only its tunnel /32, never its site network. The hub relays encrypted wg_mesh packets and must not be able to decrypt site traffic.

The hub's wg_mesh peers have no endpoint. The hub learns each spoke's IPv6 endpoint from the spoke's keepalives, and that is what it publishes for discovery.

docs.title: 2. Let the hub forward the transit range
docs.text:
The relay works by the hub forwarding packets from one spoke's transit address to another's, in and out of wg_hub. In /etc/config/firewall on the hub, allow forwarding within the zone that holds wg_hub. If that zone is called vpn:

config rule
    option name 'wg_hub-transit'
    option src 'vpn'
    option dest 'vpn'
    option dest_ip '10.10.0.0/24'
    option target 'ACCEPT'

Setting option forward 'ACCEPT' on the zone also works. Do not narrow this to UDP: the same forward usually carries management traffic between sites.

Also accept the WireGuard ports from WAN: UDP 51830 for wg_hub and UDP 51820 for wg_mesh.

docs.title: 3. Configure each spoke
docs.text:
On spoke-a, add to /etc/config/network:

config interface 'wg_hub'
    option proto 'wireguard'
    option private_key '<spoke-a wg_hub private key>'
    list addresses '10.10.0.11/32'

config wireguard_wg_hub 'hub_transit'
    option public_key 'HubHubPublicKeyExample000000000000000000000='
    option endpoint_host '203.0.113.10'
    option endpoint_port '51830'
    list allowed_ips '10.10.0.0/24'
    option route_allowed_ips '1'
    option persistent_keepalive '25'

config interface 'wg_mesh'
    option proto 'wireguard'
    option private_key '<spoke-a wg_mesh private key>'
    option listen_port '51820'
    option mtu '1360'
    list addresses '10.20.0.11/32'

config wireguard_wg_mesh 'hub'
    option public_key 'HubMeshPublicKeyExample00000000000000000000='
    option endpoint_host '2001:db8:ff::1'
    option endpoint_port '51820'
    list allowed_ips '10.20.0.1/32'
    option route_allowed_ips '1'
    option persistent_keepalive '25'

config wireguard_wg_mesh 'spoke_b'
    option public_key 'SpokeBmeshPublicKeyExample00000000000000000='
    list allowed_ips '10.12.0.0/16'
    list allowed_ips '10.20.0.12/32'
    option route_allowed_ips '1'

The points that matter:

  • The hub's wg_hub peer holds the whole transit range (10.10.0.0/24) with a route. That is what makes a relay endpoint such as 10.10.0.12:51820 travel through wg_hub.
  • The hub is also a wg_mesh peer, with a fixed IPv6 endpoint and a keepalive. The keepalive keeps the hub's view of this spoke's IPv6 endpoint current. wgpathd never steers this peer: you give it no settings in /etc/config/wgpathd, and the check and the LuCI page show it as not steered, for its fixed endpoint.
  • Every other spoke is a wg_mesh peer with no endpoint. wgpathd sets the endpoint. What it needs to steer the peer, its relay endpoint (that spoke's transit address plus its wg_mesh listen port, here 10.10.0.12:51820) and its tunnel address (10.20.0.12, which must be in its allowed_ips), goes into /etc/config/wgpathd when you configure the spoke, not here.
  • No wg_mesh peer may include any transit address in allowed_ips. Otherwise the relay endpoint would route into wg_mesh and wgpathd would refuse to manage that peer.

spoke-b mirrors this with its own keys and addresses. Its spoke_a peer has allowed_ips 10.11.0.0/16 and 10.20.0.11/32; its relay endpoint is 10.10.0.11:51820 and its tunnel address 10.20.0.11.

docs.title: 4. Open inbound IPv6 on reachable sites
docs.text:
On each spoke that should accept direct connections (spoke-a here), accept UDP 51820 from WAN over IPv6:

config rule
    option name 'Allow-wg_mesh'
    option src 'wan'
    option family 'ipv6'
    option proto 'udp'
    option dest_port '51820'
    option target 'ACCEPT'

A roaming site behind a stateful firewall (spoke-b) needs no inbound rule. Its outgoing probes open the way.

Put wg_hub and wg_mesh in a firewall zone, vpn in the examples, as your site policy requires. A zone that holds only them keeps the rules wgpathd needs, added in the next guide, from opening anything to other networks.

docs.title: 5. Apply and check
docs.text:
Apply on each node:

service network reload
service firewall reload

Then check:

  • On the hub, wg show wg_mesh endpoints lists each spoke with an IPv6 endpoint, such as [2001:db8:a::1]:51820. This is exactly what discovery will publish.
  • On each spoke, ip route get 10.10.0.12 (the other spoke's transit address) answers dev wg_hub.
  • On each spoke, wg show wg_mesh lists the hub peer with a recent handshake, and the other spokes with no endpoint.

The spokes cannot yet reach each other over wg_mesh: their mesh peers have no endpoint until wgpathd sets one. Continue with How to open the firewall for wgpathd, then How to install wgpathd.

docs.title: How to Inspect Status and Troubleshoot
docs.text:
Three commands tell you what wgpathd is doing and what it needs:

service wgpathd status     # state of every peer
service wgpathd check      # configuration and substrate
logread -e wgpathd         # what happened

To watch every message as it happens, including routine detail, stop the service and run the daemon in the foreground, where it also writes to the terminal: service wgpathd stop; /usr/libexec/wgpathd/daemon.uc. Press Ctrl+C and run service wgpathd start when done.

ubus call wgpathd status has every field, such as up_streak, ready and backoff. The output of each is described in Service commands, ubus status and Log messages. This guide goes from symptom to cause.

docs.title: The service is not running
docs.text:
service wgpathd status does not print running.

  1. If it prints disabled (option enabled in /etc/config/wgpathd), set option enabled '1' and run service wgpathd start.
  2. Run service wgpathd check and fix every FAIL line. start refuses a configuration that fails the check, and says so with invalid configuration, not starting; nothing retries it.
  3. If the check passes, look at the last lines of logread -e wgpathd. A startup failed: line names the problem as an error code, and procd retries every 5 seconds.
    • INTERFACE_MISSING: the interface is not up; check ubus call wireguard status.
    • PUBLISHER_LISTEN_FAILED on a hub: serve_addr is not assigned on this host, often because wg_hub is down, or another process holds the port.
  4. Fix the cause and run service wgpathd start.

docs.title: A peer is missing from peers
docs.text:
The peer is not managed. Find it under unmanaged in the status, or in the peer lines of service wgpathd check; the reason says why. The reasons are listed in Managed and unmanaged peers.

  • not configured: the peer has no peer section in /etc/config/wgpathd, or its public_key there differs from the one in /etc/config/network. Add or fix it as in How to configure a spoke, then run service wgpathd reload. If service wgpathd check warns about options left over in /etc/config/network, see How to upgrade from a release that kept peer settings in the network configuration.
  • fixed endpoint: as not configured, for a peer with an endpoint_host in /etc/config/network. For the hub peer that is right, and nothing needs fixing. For another spoke, add its peer section: wgpathd then steers it in place of the fixed endpoint.
  • configured more than once: two peer sections have the peer's key. Remove one, then run service wgpathd reload.
  • missing ... or invalid ...: fix the relay or tunnel of the peer's peer section in /etc/config/wgpathd (or its public_key in /etc/config/network), then run service wgpathd reload.
  • relay routes into wg_mesh: some wg_mesh peer's allowed_ips covers the relay address. Remove it and make sure the hub's wg_hub peer holds the transit range. Check with ip route get <relay address>; it must say dev wg_hub, and service wgpathd check must show the peer as ok. Then run service wgpathd reload: the reload guards the peer again and logs peer <section> (<key prefix>): relay route found, now managed.
  • relay route lookup failed: ...: usually wg_hub was not up yet. wgpathd retries every cycle and logs relay route found, now managed when it succeeds.

A managed peer that is missing from the kernel's peer table is skipped and logged as absent from wg_mesh, skipped. Check wg show wg_mesh; the peer returns to normal once netifd has it again, logged as back in wg_mesh.

docs.title: A peer never becomes ready
docs.text:
up_streak stays at 0 and ready stays false. The peer has no direct evidence.

  • Roamer side (it should reach an anchor):
    • Discovery is stale (discovery.fresh is false): the spoke cannot fetch from the hub. See discovery failed: lines in the log, and try uclient-fetch -qO- <discovery URL>. A Connection refused usually means the hub's firewall rejects the port: service wgpathd check on the hub says so in its firewall: line.
    • The peer's key is not in the hub's published list: the hub has no IPv6 endpoint for it, or none that could be a direct path. On the hub, check service wgpathd status.
    • candidate_refused is set: this router will not take the published address, and the log says why in candidate refused endpoint=<endpoint> reason=<reason>. An own address or routes into <iface> usually means a route or an address on this router covers the peer's public address; see Discovery HTTP API.
    • ping -6 <peer IPv6 address> fails: the peer's host does not answer ICMPv6 echo, for example because its firewall lost OpenWrt's Allow-ICMPv6-Input (its service wgpathd check says so), or the address is stale.
  • Anchor side: an anchor usually cannot ping a roamer behind a stateful firewall. Its evidence comes from the roamer's direct packets. Make sure the roamer is in steer mode and has reached DIRECT.
  • Neither side is inbound-reachable: the pair stays on the relay. That is the intended result.

docs.title: A peer is ready but never trials
docs.text:
• mode is observe. Trials only happen in steer mode: How to move a spoke from observe to steer. In observe mode the log says ready, steer would trial endpoint=<endpoint> when a peer becomes ready.
  • backoff is not 0: a trial waits until the backoff since the last failure has passed. ready can be true in the meantime.

docs.title: Trials time out
docs.text:
The log shows transition TRIALING -> RELAY reason=trial_timeout backoff=<s>s again and again, with the backoff growing, until the address is given up.

The direct endpoint answers ping, but WireGuard traffic does not get through both ways. Common causes:

  • The anchor does not accept UDP 51820 from WAN over IPv6.
  • The endpoint published by the hub has a port that does not reach the peer's wg_mesh, for example because of port translation.
  • The peer does not answer the tunnel probe: its firewall does not accept ICMP echo requests from the zone of its wg_mesh. Run service wgpathd check on the peer: its firewall: line for the tunnel probe says so, with the rule to add. See How to open the firewall for wgpathd.
  • One direction is broken. The trial needs a round trip, so one-way loss correctly fails it.
  • The path drops large packets. The tunnel probe fills the wg_mesh MTU, so a direct path that only carries smaller packets, for example over a link with a lower MTU that drops what does not fit, fails the trial. Lower the wg_mesh MTU on both sides until full-size packets cross, or leave the peer on the relay.
  • The other side is in RELAY and sends a lot of traffic through the relay. Its packets move this side's endpoint back onto the relay, and an answer that comes back that way does not count. On a healthy path a trial still gets through between those packets, and the other side then trials on the roam; if it is held by its own backoff, this side waits for that backoff to run out.

Each failed trial also cuts that peer's traffic for up to trial_window. After give_up_after of them in a row (3) on the same address, wgpathd stops testing it; see What a trial costs.

docs.title: The direct address is given up
docs.text:
The log shows direct address given up endpoint=<endpoint> failed_trials=<n> pause=<s>s, and given_up is set for the peer in ubus call wgpathd status. After give_up_after trials in a row on that address timed out, wgpathd stopped testing it on the underlay echo alone, so the peer's traffic no longer pays for a failed trial every backoff. The peer stays on the relay; up_streak goes on counting the echo answers, but ready stays false.

It tests again by itself, logged as direct address trials resumed reason=<reason>, when:

  • the peer's packets arrive directly, for example when the other side tests the path (roam),
  • the hub publishes another address for the peer that answers ping (new_candidate),
  • the time in given_up.until has passed, give_up_pause after the give-up, 6 hours by default (pause_over). This is one trial: if it fails, the address is given up again at once.

Once you have fixed the cause, one of those in Trials time out, you need not wait: service wgpathd restart forgets the give-up, and the peer earns direct again from scratch. A reload keeps it. To give up sooner or later, see How to tune timing parameters.

docs.title: A peer keeps falling back
docs.text:
The log alternates reason=trial_ok and transition DIRECT -> RELAY reason=demoted. The direct path passes a trial, then loses m_down tunnel probes in a row.

wgpathd already damps this: each demotion doubles the backoff up to 15 minutes, so a flapping path ends up parked on the relay. If the path is merely lossy, raising m_down makes it more tolerant. See How to tune timing parameters.

docs.title: Endpoints change on every cycle
docs.text: wg show wg_mesh endpoints flips between the relay and a direct address while the status says RELAY. This is normal when the other side is DIRECT and this side is not yet: this side re-asserts the relay each cycle, and the other side's direct packets roam it back. This side trials on the first such roam, so it ends within a cycle or two, or stays like this while its backoff runs. Both directions keep working. While it lasts, this side's own traffic reaches the other side through the relay and roams that side back as well, which shows there as a growing relayed_answers.

docs.title: Both sides are DIRECT but traffic still uses the relay
docs.text:
Both peers show DIRECT, yet wg show wg_mesh endpoints keeps showing the relay on one side or both, and relayed_answers in ubus call wgpathd status grows every cycle. Site-to-site latency sits between the direct and the relay figures.

This is WireGuard's roaming, not a wgpathd fault. Its endpoint follows the last authenticated packet, from whichever path. When both sides switch from the relay to direct while traffic flows steadily between them, packets already on their way through the relay arrive after the switch, since the relay is slower, and move the endpoint back. Each side then sends through the relay again, and moves the other one back in turn. wgpathd re-asserts the direct endpoint every cycle, but steady traffic with no pause longer than the relay's extra latency can keep the two bouncing for as long as it lasts. In the lab, with 20 ms added to the relay round trip and a steady 100 packets/s, it did not settle within two minutes.

Nothing is lost: all traffic still arrives, part of it over the relay. It ends at the first pause in the traffic. If it persists, check that the direct path is really healthy: a direct path that died while the peer was DIRECT looks the same, since relayed answers still hold DIRECT (see Relay traffic and the proof). A short pause in the traffic, or service wgpathd restart on one side, tells the two apart: on a healthy path the endpoints settle on the direct addresses.

docs.title: The log shows an outage
docs.text:
Repeated failures are logged once, when they start, and again with recovered when they end. A failed line with no recovered after it means the problem is still there.

  • discovery failed:: the spoke cannot fetch from the hub. Fix discovery, or wait while the hub is down; direct paths that work are not affected.
  • watchdog ping failed:: procd does not know the service. This happens when the daemon is started by hand instead of through service wgpathd start.
  • saving the discovery cache failed:: /var/run/wgpathd cannot be written, usually because the tmpfs is full. The payload is used all the same.
  • setting endpoints on <iface> failed:: the cycle's single wg set failed, so no endpoint was set and no tunnel probe was sent. Check that wg is installed and the interface exists.
  • reading the MTU of <iface> failed:: the mesh interface is missing, so no tunnel probe could be sized or sent.
  • sending probes failed:: a probe could not be sent, for example because the mesh interface was being recreated or a probe did not fit the route's MTU.

docs.title: How to Tune Timing Parameters
docs.text: The defaults suit a few sites on ordinary broadband: leave a dead direct path in roughly 8 to 15 seconds, and return to direct after about 15 to 20 seconds of evidence plus a trial. Change them only when you have a reason, such as a lab where you want faster transitions, or a path that flaps.

docs.title: Set a parameter
docs.text:
Each parameter is an option in the main section of /etc/config/wgpathd. For example, to require 10 cycles of evidence instead of 5:

uci set wgpathd.main.n_up='10'
uci commit wgpathd
service wgpathd reload

The running daemon applies the new value from its next cycle, and peers keep their state.

To go back to the default, delete the option:

uci delete wgpathd.main.n_up
uci commit wgpathd
service wgpathd reload

Each parameter has bounds, and a spoke's parameters must agree with each other (see below). A value outside them is refused: the reload prints a line such as FAIL config: option cycle must be a number from 1 to 10 and the daemon keeps its current values. service wgpathd check shows the same line before you reload. All names, defaults and exact semantics are in Timing parameters.

docs.title: Common adjustments
docs.text:
Fall back faster or slower. A cycle lasts cycle plus the time its probes wait, and on a dead path the tunnel probe waits for its timeout: with the defaults a cycle then takes about 4 seconds. A dead path is left after m_down to m_down + 1 such cycles. Lower m_down to 1 to fall back on the first missed probe; raise it if a lossy link causes needless fallbacks.

Return to direct more cautiously. Raise n_up to demand a longer run of evidence, and raise backoff_min so a failed trial or a fallback waits longer before the next attempt.

Park a flapping path sooner or longer. The backoff doubles from backoff_min up to backoff_max with each failure, and only resets after backoff_reset seconds of stable DIRECT. Raise backoff_max to hold a bad path on the relay longer; lower backoff_reset to forgive a path sooner.

Stop testing an address that never carries WireGuard, sooner or later. After give_up_after failed trials in a row (3) on the same address, wgpathd stops testing it on the echo alone for give_up_pause (6 hours), since each failed trial loses that peer's traffic for up to trial_window. Lower give_up_pause if a firewall on the path is fixed often and you do not want to wait for the other side, a new address or a restart to bring the peer back; raise give_up_after for a path whose trials fail now and then although it works. give_up_after 100 all but turns giving up off, leaving the backoff alone to space the trials. See Giving up an address.

Pick up roaming peers faster. Lower discovery_interval. Peers stuck in RELAY without evidence already trigger a refresh at most every 10 seconds, so this mostly helps peers that are DIRECT or have evidence.

Speed everything up for a lab. For example:

config wgpathd 'main'
    ...
    option cycle 1
    option n_up 3
    option trial_window 3
    option backoff_min 5
    option backoff_max 20
    option backoff_reset 30
    option discovery_interval 10

docs.title: Keep these relationships
docs.text:
On a spoke, wgpathd refuses two combinations, whichever of the values you set:

  • trial_window must be longer than cycle plus tunnel_timeout, or even a good path would fail its trial. So raising cycle or tunnel_timeout may mean raising trial_window too: cycle 8 needs a trial_window above 9. The tunnel probe answer is read one cycle after it is sent, and the deadline is checked first. A second attempt fits only if two cycles, including their probe waits, end before the deadline. With the defaults they usually do not, so a trial normally stands or falls on its first probe.
  • backoff_max must be at least backoff_min. Raising backoff_min above 900 therefore means raising backoff_max with it.

Keep the others in mind yourself:

  • tunnel_timeout must exceed the round-trip time of the slowest direct path, or answers arrive too late and count as lost. Fractions work: 0.5 waits half a second. Raise it only for a path whose replies are slow: a cycle waits for its probes, so while a path is dead each cycle takes up to tunnel_timeout longer, or twice that when some peers are in RELAY (their underlay probes) and others trialing or DIRECT (their tunnel probes).
  • procd restarts the daemon if 30 seconds pass without a watchdog ping, and the daemon pings once per cycle. The upper bounds of cycle (10) and tunnel_timeout (5) keep the longest cycle within that; see Timing parameters.

The hub uses only cycle, as its snapshot interval.

docs.title: How to Remove wgpathd
docs.text: Removing wgpathd leaves your WireGuard interfaces as they are, including whatever endpoint it last set on each mesh peer.

docs.title: 1. Decide where the peers should be left
docs.text:
When wgpathd stops, each mesh peer keeps its last endpoint until something changes it. A peer left on a direct endpoint keeps working only while that direct path does; nothing will fall back to the relay any more.

To leave every managed peer on the relay first, switch the spoke to observe and let it run for one cycle:

uci set wgpathd.main.mode='observe'
uci commit wgpathd
service wgpathd reload
sleep 5

docs.title: 2. Remove the package
docs.text:
apk del wgpathd

Removing the package stops and disables the service, and reloads rpcd, which drops the wgpathd.config ubus object. It leaves the firewall as it is.

docs.title: 3. Clean up leftovers
docs.text:
Remove the runtime cache on a spoke:

rm -rf /var/run/wgpathd

If /etc/config/wgpathd is still there after removal, delete it.

The traffic rules you added for wgpathd stay in /etc/config/firewall. Remove them if nothing else needs them: the ones named Allow-wgpathd-* in Network → Firewall → Traffic Rules, or with uci delete on their sections, then uci commit firewall and service firewall reload. Keep Allow-ICMPv6-Input, which is OpenWrt's own.

wgpathd keeps nothing in /etc/config/network. If the router ran a release up to 4 and its settings were never moved, the wgpathd_relay and wgpathd_tunnel options may still be there: netifd ignores them, so they can stay, or you can remove them for a clean file.

docs.title: Afterwards
docs.text: Mesh peers without an endpoint in /etc/config/network get none after the next service network reload or reboot, so spoke-to-spoke traffic over wg_mesh stops until you give them one. Set a static endpoint_host and endpoint_port on those peers if you want them to keep working without wgpathd.

docs.title: How to Upgrade from a Release That Kept Peer Settings in the Network Configuration
docs.text:
Releases up to 4 kept each steered peer's relay endpoint and tunnel address as the options wgpathd_relay and wgpathd_tunnel of its section in /etc/config/network. Later releases read them from a peer section of /etc/config/wgpathd instead, keyed by the peer's public key, and ignore the old options.

The package moves them for you. This guide shows how to check that it did, and how to do it by hand if it could not.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A spoke that runs a release up to 4 with its peers steered.
  • The new package, built and copied to the router as in How to install wgpathd.
  • The firewall rules of How to open the firewall for wgpathd, added on every node.

Add the firewall rules before you upgrade

Releases up to 5 loaded wgpathd's firewall accepts themselves, and the upgrade removes them from the running firewall. Without the rules added first, a zone that rejects input rejects the probes, relayed packets and peer list as soon as the upgrade finishes, and the peers lose their direct paths, and possibly the relay.

docs.title: 1. Upgrade the package
docs.text:
apk add --allow-untrusted /tmp/wgpathd-0.1.0-r*.apk

During the upgrade, the package's post-upgrade script, through OpenWrt's default_postinst, runs /etc/uci-defaults/50-wgpathd-peers, which runs /usr/libexec/wgpathd/migrate.uc. For each WireGuard peer section in /etc/config/network with either option, it:

  1. adds a peer section with that section's public_key to /etc/config/wgpathd, or completes the one already there, as relay and tunnel;
  2. commits /etc/config/wgpathd;
  3. deletes wgpathd_relay and wgpathd_tunnel from the network section, and commits /etc/config/network.

Only then does the script restart the running daemon, so it starts with the moved settings. A value /etc/config/wgpathd already holds is kept, and no copy of /etc/config/network is written.

docs.title: 2. Check the result
docs.text:
logread -e 'migrate:'

Sun Sep 27 16:02:11 2026 daemon.notice wgpathd[2210]: migrate: moved the settings of 1 peer(s) from /etc/config/network to /etc/config/wgpathd

The settings are now in /etc/config/wgpathd, and gone from /etc/config/network:

uci show wgpathd | grep '@peer'
grep wgpathd_ /etc/config/network

The first command prints a public_key, relay and tunnel for each steered peer; the second prints nothing. Then run the check:

service wgpathd check

Each peer you steered before has an ok peer line, no line says left over from an earlier version, and every firewall: line is ok.

docs.title: If it could not move them
docs.text:
The log says why:

  • migrate: failed, /etc/config/network left as it was: MIGRATE_FAILED (<detail>): a file could not be read or written; the details are in Error codes. /etc/config/network is unchanged, and /etc/uci-defaults/50-wgpathd-peers is kept, so it runs again at the next boot. After fixing the cause, run it at once with service wgpathd migrate, then service wgpathd reload.
  • migrate: network section <section> has no valid public_key, its options stay: that section cannot be keyed. Fix its public_key, then run service wgpathd migrate and service wgpathd reload.
  • migrate: network section <section>: kept relay '<value>' of /etc/config/wgpathd, dropped wgpathd_relay '<value>': /etc/config/wgpathd already had a different value, which wins. If the dropped one was right, set it with uci set and reload.

Until the settings are moved, the peers are not configured, or fixed endpoint for one with an endpoint_host: wgpathd leaves their endpoints alone, and the check and the log at startup name every network section still holding the old options.

docs.title: To move them by hand
docs.text:
For each peer section that still has the options, spoke_b here, copy them into a new peer section, commit /etc/config/wgpathd, and only then remove them from /etc/config/network:

uci add wgpathd peer
uci set wgpathd.@peer[-1].public_key="$(uci get network.spoke_b.public_key)"
uci set wgpathd.@peer[-1].relay="$(uci get network.spoke_b.wgpathd_relay)"
uci set wgpathd.@peer[-1].tunnel="$(uci get network.spoke_b.wgpathd_tunnel)"
uci commit wgpathd

uci delete network.spoke_b.wgpathd_relay
uci delete network.spoke_b.wgpathd_tunnel
uci commit network

Skip uci add for a peer that already has a peer section: two sections with one key leave the peer unsteered, configured more than once. Then check and apply:

service wgpathd check
service wgpathd reload

service wgpathd migrate does the same for every peer at once.

docs.title: How to Write Documentation
docs.text: The documentation is built with MkDocs Material, inside Docker. You need Docker and make.

docs.title: Preview while you write
docs.text:
make -C docs serve

Open http://localhost:8000. The page reloads when you save a file under docs/ or change mkdocs.yml. make docs-serve from the repository root does the same. If port 8000 is taken, for example by another project's preview, choose another: make -C docs serve DOCS_PORT=8001.

docs.title: Build the site
docs.text:
make -C docs build

make docs from the repository root does the same. The site goes to bin/site/, and make -C docs clean removes it.

The build runs mkdocs build --strict, so a broken link or any other warning fails it. CI runs the same strict build on pushes and pull requests to main that touch the docs, and a second one with the versioned config, mkdocs.mike.yml (make -C docs build-mike locally).

Merging to main publishes nothing: the docs go online with the next release. To correct the docs already online, see How to fix the docs of the released version; what publishes when is in Documentation publishing.

docs.title: Where a page goes
docs.text:
Pick the folder by what the reader is doing, following Diátaxis:

Folder The reader is... Example tutorials/ learning by doing, guided step by step Developer onboarding how-to/ working toward a goal they already have Configure a spoke reference/ looking up a fact Every status field explanation/ trying to understand why The state machine

Keep one type per page and link to the others instead of mixing them. Add every new page to nav in mkdocs.yml and to the index.md of its folder. Link between pages with relative paths, never with the site's URL, so each published version links to itself.

Design notes and build logs are not kept in the repository. The reasoning a reader needs lives in the explanation pages: when a change rests on a new reason, write it there, in the same change, rather than pointing to a record outside the site. Code and test comments follow the same rule: give the reason in a few words, or point to the explanation page that holds it.

docs.title: Keep it true
docs.text:
Reference pages describe the code as it is. When you change an option, parameter, status field, log message, error code, HTTP behavior or installed file, update the matching reference page in the same change:

Code Reference page config.uc, files/etc/config/wgpathd UCI configuration, WireGuard substrate params.uc Timing parameters daemon.uc status ubus status publisher.uc, discovery.uc Discovery HTTP API deps.log(...) calls Log messages errors.uc Error codes files/etc/init.d/wgpathd, check.uc, status_view.uc, daemon reload Service commands rpc.uc, candidate.uc ubus config check migrate.uc, files/etc/uci-defaults/ Files and dependencies, How to upgrade peer settings files/, openwrt/wgpathd/Makefile Files and dependencies firewall.uc, the firewall findings of check.uc Firewall rules, Service commands, How to open the firewall root Makefile Make targets luci/ pages, menu and ACL Files and dependencies, How to check mesh paths in LuCI, How to configure mesh paths in LuCI docs/Makefile, devenv/scripts/docs-*.sh, .github/workflows/docs.yml, mkdocs.mike.yml, docs/overrides/, devenv/gh-pages/, devenv/services/docs/ Make targets, Documentation publishing

docs.title: Diagrams and examples
docs.text:
• Use Mermaid in a fenced block with the mermaid language. Add a diagram only where a picture explains more than a paragraph.
  • Use generic names (hub, spoke-a, spoke-b) and documentation addresses: 2001:db8::/32 for IPv6, 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 for public IPv4. Never use real site names, keys or public addresses.
  • Output captured from the e2e lab is the exception: paste it as it is. Its private addresses and keys are disposable and match what the reader sees when they run the lab.

docs.title: How to Fix the Docs of the Released Version
docs.text: A docs fix reaches the published site through the docs branch of the newest minor, docs/X.Y: pushing the branch republishes /X.Y/. Only the newest minor gets fixes; older versions stay as they are. The examples fix 0.2.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The fix is merged into main. Fixes always land on main first.
  • The fix changes only files under docs/, mkdocs.yml or mkdocs.mike.yml. A code fix needs a release instead: How to publish the docs of a patch release.

docs.title: 1. Cherry-pick the fix onto the docs branch
docs.text:
git fetch origin --tags
git switch docs/0.2
git cherry-pick <sha>

Cherry-pick each commit you need. Never merge or rebase main into docs/0.2: it would publish the docs of unreleased work (why).

If a commit also changes files outside the docs, take only its docs part:

git cherry-pick -n <sha>
git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree -- . ':!docs/' ':!mkdocs.yml' ':!mkdocs.mike.yml'
git commit -C <sha>

docs.title: 2. Check the branch
docs.text:
devenv/scripts/docs-guard.sh docs/0.2

It prints the release tag when the branch may publish. If it refuses, see below.

docs.title: 3. Push
docs.text:
git push origin docs/0.2

The docs workflow republishes /0.2/. Check that its publish job succeeded.

docs.title: If the guard refuses
docs.text:
The message tells you which case you are in; every message is listed in Docs-only guard.

  • docs/0.2 changes files outside docs/: <files>; code fixes need a release: a commit on the branch changes code. If you have not pushed yet, drop it with git reset --hard origin/docs/0.2 and cherry-pick again as in step 1. If it is already pushed, revert it and push the revert:

    git revert <sha>
git push origin docs/0.2

    The code fix ships with the next release.

  • v0.2.1 is not an ancestor of docs/0.2: a patch release was tagged and the branch has not moved to it. Move it as in How to publish the docs of a patch release, then push again.

  • docs/0.2 has no v0.2.* release tag: the tags are missing locally. Run git fetch origin --tags. In CI, the minor has not been released yet, and the branch should not exist.

docs.title: How to Build the Package
docs.text: The packages are built in the official OpenWrt SDK image, inside Docker. The result is two architecture-independent .apk files with the same version: wgpathd, the daemon, and luci-app-wgpathd, its LuCI pages.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
make package

The first run builds a wgpathd-sdk image from ghcr.io/openwrt/sdk and updates the feed metadata (base, packages and luci), which takes a while. The packages land in bin/:

bin/wgpathd-0.1.0-r8.apk
bin/luci-app-wgpathd-0.1.0-r8.apk

For the full SDK build output, add VERBOSE=1.

The build mounts openwrt/wgpathd/Makefile, src/, files/ and luci/ read-only into the SDK. Only the metadata of the runtime dependencies is used; none of them are compiled.

docs.title: Check the package
docs.text:
make package-check

This builds the packages and a check image (the pinned rootfs plus both packages' dependencies, including luci-base, and quickjs), then installs the daemon offline in a container with no network and NET_ADMIN in its own empty network namespace, and checks that:

  • it installs without fetching anything, and the service start during install does nothing;
  • every file is in place with the right mode, nothing is installed on the PATH, there is no uci-defaults script, and /etc/config/wgpathd is a conffile shipped with enabled '0';
  • the modules load from the default ucode search path;
  • daemon.uc and check.uc --config with the shipped configuration, and status.uc with no daemon, fail with a one-line reason rather than a ucode stack trace;
  • the full check.uc passes a valid hub configuration without ubus, and prints the firewall rule that hub needs;
  • a real rpcd serves wgpathd.config from the plugin, and its check reads /etc/config/firewall and reports a missing rule with the rule to add;
  • the init script enables, and the package ships no firewall rule and loads none;
  • the package scripts reload rpcd on install, upgrade and removal, may reload the firewall only on install and upgrade, restart a running daemon on upgrade, and parse;
  • luci-app-wgpathd depends on exactly the daemon's version, and apk refuses it next to any other wgpathd release;
  • the app installs on top of the daemon, ships only its menu, ACL and two views with mode 0644, the menu and ACL parse as JSON, the views parse as JavaScript (with quickjs, as the function body LuCI compiles them into), and its scripts parse;
  • installing and removing the app clear LuCI's menu and module caches, and removing it keeps the daemon;
  • the daemon package removes cleanly;
  • an upgrade from a release that shipped the fw4 include, simulated in apk's database, removes the file and unloads its four rules.

The last line is package-check: all passed, or the number of failed checks. The container runs no procd or ubusd, so starting the service and the ubus object are out of its reach.

docs.title: Build for another release
docs.text:
make package OPENWRT_VERSION=25.12.5
make package-check OPENWRT_VERSION=25.12.5

OPENWRT_VERSION and OPENWRT_ARCH select the SDK and rootfs image tags. The package is the same for every architecture.

docs.title: Change what is packaged
docs.text:
• Version and release: PKG_VERSION and PKG_RELEASE in openwrt/wgpathd/Makefile.
  • Dependencies: DEPENDS in each package's define Package/<name> block of the same file. The root Makefile reads the daemon's to install the same dependencies into the test image, so tests always run against them, and both to build the package-check image.
  • Installed files: the Package/wgpathd/install and Package/luci-app-wgpathd/install sections. The app installs everything under luci/htdocs into /www and everything under luci/root into /. When you add a file, add a matching check to devenv/scripts/package-check.sh and a row to Files and dependencies.

docs.title: How to Publish the Docs of a New Minor Release
docs.text: A new minor release, such as 0.2.0, publishes its docs as /0.2/ and moves /latest/ to them. It also starts a new docs branch and freezes the previous one. The examples release 0.2.0 after 0.1.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Publishing is set up: How to set up documentation publishing.
  • The release is ready on main, with PKG_VERSION:=0.2.0 in openwrt/wgpathd/Makefile.
  • Every pinned docs link in the shipped files points to /0.2/, including URL:= in openwrt/wgpathd/Makefile. If the project keeps a CHANGELOG.md, the release's entries are under ## [0.2.0]. make lint passes.

docs.title: 1. Tag the release
docs.text:
git tag v0.2.0
git push origin v0.2.0

The docs workflow publishes /0.2/, titled 0.2.0, and moves latest to it. Check that its publish job succeeded and that /latest/ shows 0.2.0 in the version selector.

docs.title: 2. Create the docs branch
docs.text:
git branch docs/0.2 v0.2.0
git push origin docs/0.2

docs.title: 3. Freeze the previous branch
docs.text:
Stop pushing to docs/0.1. /0.1/ stays online as it was last published. From now on, doc fixes go to docs/0.2: see How to fix the docs of the released version.

What each push publishes, and when latest moves, is in Documentation publishing. Why only the newest minor gets fixes: About versioned documentation.

docs.title: How to Publish the Docs of a Patch Release
docs.text: A patch release, such as 0.2.1, republishes its minor, /0.2/, from the new tag. Afterwards the docs branch has to move onto the tag, or it cannot publish again. The examples release 0.2.1.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The minor's docs branch exists: How to publish the docs of a new minor release.
  • The release is ready, with PKG_VERSION:=0.2.1 in openwrt/wgpathd/Makefile, and make lint passes.

docs.title: 1. Tag the release
docs.text:
git tag v0.2.1
git push origin v0.2.1

The docs workflow republishes /0.2/, now titled 0.2.1. latest follows if 0.2 is the newest minor.

docs.title: 2. Move the docs branch to the tag
docs.text:
git fetch origin
git switch docs/0.2
git merge --ff-only v0.2.1

If the fast-forward fails because the branch has fix commits of its own, merge the tag instead:

git merge v0.2.1

If the merge conflicts, keep the tag's side for every file outside docs/, mkdocs.yml and mkdocs.mike.yml: the branch may only differ from the tag in the docs.

Then push:

git push origin docs/0.2

Until the branch contains v0.2.1, every publish from it is refused with v0.2.1 is not an ancestor of docs/0.2. See Docs-only guard.

docs.title: How to Republish a Version
docs.text: Republish a version when its publish failed or was cancelled, or when gh-pages lost it. The docs workflow can be run by hand for any release tag or docs branch. The examples republish 0.2.

docs.title: 1. Choose the ref
docs.text:
• If the minor has a docs branch, use it: docs/0.2. It holds the release plus its doc fixes.
  • Otherwise use the minor's newest release tag, for example v0.2.1.

Republishing an older tag than the newest, or a tag instead of the branch, replaces /0.2/ with older docs.

docs.title: 2. Run the workflow
docs.text:
In the repository, open Actions → docs → Run workflow, enter the ref, and run it. With the GitHub CLI:

gh workflow run docs.yml -f ref=docs/0.2

Republishing an older minor leaves latest on the newest one. A docs branch still has to pass the docs-only guard; if it refuses, see How to fix the docs of the released version.

docs.title: How to Set Up Documentation Publishing
docs.text: Nothing is published until the repository is on GitHub, the site's URL is known, and the first release is tagged. Do these steps once, in this order. The examples use https://<user>.github.io/wgpathd/ as the site's URL and 0.1.0 as the first release.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A GitHub repository for wgpathd, with admin rights to change its Pages settings.
  • The first release, 0.1.0, is ready on main: PKG_VERSION:=0.1.0 in openwrt/wgpathd/Makefile.

docs.title: 1. Push main
docs.text:
git remote add origin git@github.com:<user>/wgpathd.git
git push -u origin main

docs.title: 2. Set the site's URL and pin the links
docs.text:
1. In mkdocs.yml, set site_url to the site's base URL, without a version:

    site_url: https://<user>.github.io/wgpathd/

  2. In openwrt/wgpathd/Makefile, point URL:= to the docs of the package's minor:

    URL:=https://<user>.github.io/wgpathd/0.1/

  3. Link the README to https://<user>.github.io/wgpathd/latest/.

  4. Check the pinned links:

    make lint

Commit the change and push it to main. Which link goes where is in Links to the documentation.

docs.title: 3. Tag the first release
docs.text:
git tag v0.1.0
git push origin v0.1.0

The docs workflow creates gh-pages and publishes /0.1/ and /latest/. Wait for its publish job to succeed.

docs.title: 4. Turn on GitHub Pages
docs.text: In the repository's Settings → Pages, set the source to Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). The site then answers at https://<user>.github.io/wgpathd/, which redirects to /latest/.

docs.title: 5. Create the docs branch
docs.text:
git branch docs/0.1 v0.1.0
git push origin docs/0.1

Doc fixes for 0.1 go through this branch: see How to fix the docs of the released version.

docs.title: Clear an unversioned deploy from gh-pages
docs.text:
If gh-pages carries files from an earlier unversioned deploy, for example from mkdocs gh-deploy, remove them once: they shadow the 404 redirect and keep serving stale pages. Do it while no docs workflow is running.

  1. Check out gh-pages and list its root:

    git fetch origin gh-pages
git switch gh-pages
git ls-tree --name-only HEAD

  2. Remove everything that is not part of the versioned layout: the version folders, latest, versions.json, index.html, 404.html and .nojekyll stay.

    git ls-tree --name-only HEAD |
    grep -vxE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+|latest|versions\.json|index\.html|404\.html|\.nojekyll' |
    xargs git rm -r -q
git commit -m 'Remove the unversioned site'
git push origin gh-pages
git switch main

If gh-pages has not been published with mike yet, publish first (step 3), so that index.html is mike's redirect and not the old site's home page.

docs.title: How to Run the Tests
docs.text: All tests run in a pinned OpenWrt rootfs container with utest. You need Docker and make; nothing else is installed on the host.

docs.title: Run everything
docs.text:
make test

This runs the unit suite (test/unit) and the integration suite (test/integration). The first run builds the wgpathd-openwrt image, which takes a few minutes.

To run one suite:

make unit
make integration

docs.title: Narrow it down
docs.text:
Run tests whose name matches a regular expression:

make unit FILTER='trial'

Run specific files or directories:

make unit MODULES=test/unit/wgpathd/decide_test.uc
make test MODULES='test/unit/wgpathd/config_test.uc test/integration/daemon_test.uc'

See one line per test, with the failing assertion:

make test VERBOSE=1

The variables combine.

docs.title: Re-run on every change
docs.text:
make watch

This runs all tests, then again each time a file under src/, test/ or files/ changes. FILTER and MODULES apply. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Lint
docs.text:
make lint

This compiles every ucode file, including the scripts in files/usr/libexec/wgpathd/, runs sh -n on the init script and the devenv scripts, parses the LuCI JSON and scripts, fails on LuCI code that could turn data into markup (innerHTML and the like, or %s in a .format() template), and checks pinned documentation links (see Link check). CI runs make lint and make test on every push.

docs.title: Test the docs tooling
docs.text:
make docs-test

This runs test/docs/ in the docs tools image, without network: the version, guard, publish and link-check scripts in devenv/scripts/docs-*.sh, with docs-publish.sh deploying three releases through mike to a throwaway local repository, and the redirect in devenv/gh-pages/404.html under Node. The first run builds the wgpathd-docs image. CI runs it on pull requests and pushes to main that touch the docs or their tooling.

docs.title: Run the browser tests
docs.text:
make browser
make browser FILTER='hub'

This builds both packages, then runs the Playwright tests in test/browser/ against the LuCI pages: Status → Mesh paths, the Status → Overview section, Network → Mesh paths, hostile text in every free-text field, and the path strip in five themes. The first run builds the wgpathd-luci and wgpathd-browser images.

LuCI runs in an OpenWrt rootfs container with the built packages, started by hand without procd. A fake wgpathd ubus object (devenv/services/luci/fake-wgpathd.uc) answers ubus call wgpathd status with a fixture from test/fixtures/luci/, which each test chooses; the fixture none withdraws the object, as when the daemon is not running. The fixtures freeze now, so every age and wait on the page is fixed. An integration test in test/integration/daemon_test.uc checks that each fixture has the fields and value types of the daemon's own reply, so a change to the reply fails make test until the fixtures follow it.

wgpathd.config is not faked: rpcd serves it with the package's own plugin, so the settings page, its ACL and the plugin are tested together. The fake's wgpathd.fixture config writes /etc/config/network and /etc/config/wgpathd from a directory of test/fixtures/luci/config/, and read returns them as saved, which the tests compare after Save & Apply. The container also has the login meshadmin (password meshadmin), granted only rpcd's unauthenticated group, luci-base and luci-app-wgpathd: the tests use the settings page as that login, and check that it cannot read network.

The LuCI container runs with --network none and no capabilities, and uhttpd listens on 127.0.0.1. The Playwright container joins its network namespace (--network container:), so the browser reaches LuCI over that loopback and neither container has any other network. Both are removed when the run ends, also on failure or Ctrl+C.

Screenshots of the main states are in bin/browser/screenshots/; on failure, Playwright's screenshots and error context and the LuCI container's log are in bin/browser/.

docs.title: Update the translation template
docs.text:
make pot

Run it after adding or changing a string in _() or N_() in luci/, or a menu or ACL title, and commit luci/po/templates/wgpathd.pot with the change: make lint fails while the template is out of date. The template is written by openwrt/luci's own scanner, so it matches what upstream would generate. The scanner reads JavaScript with xgettext, which can lose its way on a regular expression literal with a quote or an unescaped / in a character class; it then warns, and make pot and make lint fail rather than drop strings. Write such a literal without them, for example \/ inside the brackets.

docs.title: Test against another OpenWrt release
docs.text:
make test OPENWRT_VERSION=25.12.5

OPENWRT_VERSION and OPENWRT_ARCH select the rootfs image. Each combination gets its own development image.

docs.title: Run the end-to-end failover suite
docs.text:
make e2e
make e2e SCENARIO=kill-direct
make e2e SCENARIO='baseline roam'

This builds the package, then boots three OpenWrt containers (hub, spoke-a, spoke-b) with procd as PID 1, installs the package in each, and runs the failover scenarios against them: steady DIRECT, relay fallback with traffic surviving, a direct path that drops full-size packets, the anchor-only estate (also under steady traffic), a dead direct path under relay traffic, crash and hang recovery, roaming, hub loss, the mixed state and observe mode. The scenarios are listed in test/e2e/README.md. A full run takes several minutes.

The containers get only NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW, share one internal docker network, and use the host kernel's WireGuard module, which the kernel loads on first use. The network is not IPv6-enabled in docker; netifd in each container configures the IPv6 addresses. An IPv6-enabled docker network would make docker switch on the host's net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding, even for an internal network.

The runner guards the host:

  • It warns about containers of other projects that are running, and refuses to start beside them with E2E_STRICT=1. It always refuses while the lab runs, since both use the same addresses.
  • It records ip monitor and the kernel log for the whole run, and tears the stack down at once if the Wi-Fi interface (wlan0, or E2E_WATCH_IFACE) goes down or the kernel log mentions it.
  • It records net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding and the interface's accept_ra before and after, and reports any change.
  • It always tears the stack down, including on failure or Ctrl+C.

Results, timings, per-failure node logs and the guard's logs are in bin/e2e/.

docs.title: Where tests go
docs.text:
• test/unit/ mirrors src/: one test file per module, with every I/O dependency replaced by a fake. The decision core is tested here, including property tests over random observation sequences.
  • test/integration/ drives the daemon shell and the publisher through daemon.create(...) with fake deps, and runs the publisher on a real loopback socket.
  • test/e2e/ holds one shell script per failover scenario, run on the host against the containers by make e2e.
  • test/browser/ holds the Playwright tests of the LuCI pages, test/fixtures/luci/ the status replies they run against, and test/fixtures/luci/config/ the configurations of the settings page tests.

For the reasoning behind the split, see Architecture.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Reference documentation is technical description of the machinery. It is information-oriented: consult it, don't read it end to end.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• UCI Configuration - Every option in /etc/config/wgpathd, per role, the peer sections of a spoke with the unmanaged reasons, and validation rules.
  • WireGuard Substrate - What wgpathd reads from /etc/config/network, and what it needs of the WireGuard setup.
  • Timing Parameters - Every timing parameter, its default and exact behavior, plus the fixed limits.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
• Service Commands - service wgpathd start, reload, status and check: behavior, output and exit status.
  • ubus Status - The wgpathd ubus object, field by field, for spoke and hub.
  • ubus Config Check - The wgpathd.config ubus object: the configuration check for saved or unsaved values, the mesh peers without their keys, and the parameter bounds.
  • Discovery HTTP API - GET /peers: payload, status codes, connection limits and spoke-side validation.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
• Log Messages - Every message, its level and what it means.
  • Error Codes - Every error code and its details.

docs.title: Package
docs.text:
• Firewall Rules - What each role needs the firewall to accept and why, and what the check can confirm. The package ships no rules.
  • Files and Dependencies - Installed files, runtime files, the init script, package scripts and dependencies.
  • Make Targets - Development targets and variables.
  • Documentation Publishing - The docs workflow, the gh-pages layout, the latest rule, the docs-only guard, the link check and the scripts behind them.

docs.title: Discovery HTTP API
docs.text: The hub serves the discovery snapshot over plain HTTP on serve_addr:serve_port. Spokes fetch it from the URL in their discovery option. This page describes both sides.

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text:
GET /peers

No query parameters, headers or body are used.

curl -s http://10.10.0.1:7780/peers

docs.title: Response body
docs.text:
A JSON object keyed by WireGuard public key. It contains every peer of the hub's read_iface whose current endpoint could be a direct path: an IPv6 address that is not unspecified (::), loopback (::1), multicast (ff00::/8), link-local (fe80::/10), IPv4-mapped (::ffff:0:0/96), IPv4-compatible (::/96), NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96, 64:ff9b:1::/48) or discard-only (100::/64). Global and unique local (fc00::/7) addresses are published. Peers with an IPv4 endpoint, another IPv6 endpoint or no endpoint are left out. With no such peers, the body is {}.

{
    "SpokeAmeshPublicKeyExample00000000000000000=": {
        "direct": "[2001:db8:a::1]:51820",
        "handshake_age": 12
    },
    "SpokeBmeshPublicKeyExample00000000000000000=": {
        "direct": "[2001:db8:b::20]:51820"
    }
}
